title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

blocks.x: THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Oral History
Interview with Wilbur B. Ware, Sr.
by Gloria L. Ware
Sides 1-2
December 18, 1977

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
We are here today to conduct an informal interview with Mr. Wilbur Ware for an Oral History series in the Smithsonian Institution's Division of Performing Arts.

This interview will be a survey of Mr. Ware's musical career and other aspects of his life that relate to that career. This is somewhat precedent setting -- and comments from certain indicators are filled with praise because such a project has finally been undertaken in such neglected areas of our music, and have finally been preserved. One cannot proclaim it is not enough, but can only acknowledge that at last it is being done.

Nothing is as surrounded with controversy as the music with an African foundation which came out of an environment American. At its most sophisticated level, it's most complex and beautiful; it's like no other on earth, and remains unmatched in its spontaneous creativity, called improvisation. This music is epitomized in the works of Duke Ellington, the acknowledged master to those who are aware of the depth, complexity and beauty of live improvisation.

Nevertheless, the controversy continues to surround the music and its creators. There are even disagreements as to what the music should be called. Perhaps these occur because of the nature of our society where we still call the
indigenous inhabitants Indians, and are still trying to decide what to call Americans of African descent. We're most confused at the level that individuals what are to call themselves.

Hidden behind the wall of indifference, and I should add it only seems indifferent, because others do not share our concerns, our point of view -- or in some lonely shack along a deserted road are the black folk of America, unsung, they sing or they play a musical instrument, despite the permanent there is gaiety trauma of poverty and the almost ubiquitous sadness; the laughter of the free human heart, and placidly defined in the face of slavery, there's a happiness which transcends mere laughter -- a total affirmation. This is the way Archie Shepp sees it.

There is a difference. Studio drummer Milt Holland Harlan from Chicago is quoted as saying when he was a young drummer how he realized how great a difference there was between black and white jazz styles. He found the black styles smoother and more musical; he wanted to know why some people played better than others. He discovered how some cultures are more rhythm and music based than others; that for some, these are inseparable from life. He even traveled to Africa, seeking the source. The controversy would disallow this difference and tell us that jazz in American music is such that the central black creative core no longer exists. But it does exist. The difference is real and not adversarial (unintelligible);
only affirmative.

Composer David Baker talks about the neglect of this music; the carelessness evident in documenting this music and putting it on good terms with others of the world's great musics. This is so perhaps because ignorance and inaccurate historical attention. It is so perhaps because of the growth of the world and the many uses of the music which obscure its origins and continuity in its original culture. It is so.
We will be talking at length with Mr. Ware, considered by his contemporaries and followers as a primary American bass innovator.
You were born in Chicago on September 8, 1923, the only son of Elijah Roger Bernard and Eleanor Broomfield Ware. Tell us when you became aware of music.

I became aware of music, maybe my 3rd or 4th year. By that I mean I was about 4 years old. There was a sanctified church next door to where we were living. I was living with my great aunt and my mother, and her children; my great aunt's children -- and this lady next door, they didn't have no children; Reverend Turner and his wife Della. I used to go over and have cookies and milk and whatnot.
And they had church services -- I can remember well; it was in the summer, and they had a band in there, and I can't say what instruments they Ware brought because I didn't recognize them.

but it was so joyful; I mean, the singing and the band playing, and it got so that Reverend Turner and his wife would take me over to the church nightly, and eventually I started living with Reverend Turner. They didn't adopt me, but my mother being young, and my father and her having split up ... so I was kind of raised by Reverend Turner.
And that was my first introduction to music. I guess around that time, radio was becoming kind of popular. I remember listening to that old show, Amos and Andy -- and to hear Amos sing "Am I Blue".

Well about that time, Mrs. Turner bought me a toy drum, and I'd go to church with her with the drum. I'd be in the benches -- I wouldn't be on the rostrum, naturally, I was quite young -- I don't think I was but 5; I don't remember well because I was going to something like a nursery school; I wasn't yet in kindergarten. And I remember that Reverend Turner had a piano up at his house, and an old C Melody saxophone and a couple of guitars, and they had -- they always had music going on.

Mrs. Turner, she played a little guitar. Reverend Turner would sit down and play at the piano, and I don't know to this day whether he had any musical education, but he knew how to play -- and he taught me little things.
So that was my first introduction; had to be in the 20's or the latter 20's.
What were some of things that he taught you - say, on the piano?

Well, I can remember he made a kind of a sound like a rink, tink, rink, tink, boom, boom, boom -- I'm singing this, like, that's the way it sounded. And he showed me how to chord in B flat, E flat. He would sit me on his lap and spread my fingers out on the keys, but like I said, there was a whole lot of music around that house.
When did you begin to play in the church?

Oh, let's see ... I was about 8 or 9 years old. And Reverend Turner had drums, too; just a snare drum and a bass drum -- with a pedal and sticks, and he told me how to beat them. And I don't know -- it came kind of natural, you might say,

So I began playing the drums in the church. By then, the church had broke up -- this had to be around 1930 -- the church was small and the congregation was small; everybody was very poor. I think they lost the big church they had with the Crash, because they had to take smaller living quarters, and like I said, I was staying with Mr. and Mrs. Turner at that time.

And I was playing. In church, we had a piano player, Mrs. Phillips, and Billy Johnson played great cymbals. We didn't have no horns, or at least I didn't see no horns over at their house -- just people clapping their hands, and
tambourines and singing. But it was a beautiful feeling -- a beautiful feeling. And that started me off.

And later, oh, maybe the middle thirties -- about '33 or '34, Reverend Turner decided to make a bass violin and he went out and got some veneer wood, some tacks and glue, and it took him a good 2 years to build that instrument, and he bought strings. The only thing, really, he had to buy were the strings and a bridge.

But it had a sound, [it was] sturdy -- and I got away from playing the drums in church and started the fiddle. He took me to church one night with him and said "You're gonna play it tonight." And him being the pastor, him sitting up in the pulpit, he showed me a few changes -- I played G, D, and C -- church songs, mostly.

And he tuned the fiddle up, like you tune a fiddle; with G, D, A and E. And if it rained, he had wooden pegs up there where he would have to twist them with his hand and take a hammer and tack it in to hold it, you know, because they would slip. The weather would get bad and the strings would stretch, and I just learned how to play across the fiddle that way. That was about the middle Thirties.

And during that time, I met some neighborhood older boys -- I was going on 10, maybe 11 -- and they had little string groups, and what you would call a tramps bands, and they'd have kazoos, and a washboard -- one fellow had a tenor guitar; I

had my home made bass. One fellow had a tin tub drum -- that's a drum that sits in an old washtub and a 5 gallon oil drum that had one of the heads cut out of it -- a whole lot of holes in it; there were some nails in it, and that was your snare drum.

It was a certain way they built it that was sturdy and had at least 3 skillets nailed to the top of the tin tub, and there are some old cats that are still around who would know about that tin tub drum. But the tramp bands at that time -- were very popular. There was a tramp band at the Cotton Club; and they started traveling around with Cab Calloway in the Cotton Club Revue -- they were out of Chicago, and I think they made a movie. I think they were in "Stormy Weather", but you couldn't recognize them. But they were quite popular.

And another group that I come up with -- I had to be about 12 then -- was the Chicago Maniacs, and they were some older boys in the neighborhood that I'm speaking of, who had 3 kazoos. The fellows had these old Victrolas -- the speakers were shaped something like a saxophone, you might say, a small saxophone and a big saxophone, that was your alto and your tenor -- and the guy who played the trumpet, he'd steal one of those brass from those old Buicks; just screw it off and stick the kazoo in there, and he had a trumpet.
And like I said, we had a washboard, tenor guitar,

tenor drum, and my home made fiddle. We had a fellow named Jake who played piano. Yeah, there was a piano. And we'd go out hustling from tavern to tavern and roadhouse to roadhouse, plus we played amateur shows all around Chicago. And win. The prize was $3, and I guess we had 8 pieces, but that was a nice piece of money during that time.

We also played the Savoy Ballroom. They had a barn-dance and they had a tramp band contest. Well, the Chicago Maniacs came out on top; maybe if some old Chicagoans could remember those days ... The Riviera Theatre used to have amateur shows -- I think this was during the time; I don't know, when was the time of that first flood? Wasn't it in Pennsylvania, a big flood, and they had benefits all over the country, and they had a benefit at the Riviera Theatre. I know Les Louis Armstrong was there.

And we played. That tramp band was something. And from the tramp band, the fellows started using guitars, trios and quartets, singing some barbershop harmony, and doing tunes like "China Boy" and "Chinatown" and "Tiger Rag". And I'm still playing this home made fiddle. At the same time, I'm going to school.
When did you tap dance?
Well, all during this time, I was tap dancing. I learned to tap dance about 1931, maybe before that -- my real father used to dance and he showed me the

timestep. And there was somebody -- in any neighborhood that you lived in, somebody -- everybody could sing or dance or do the time step; what they used to call the "B.S. Chorus"-- "Shim Sham Shimmee", and all the Bucking Wings, and Knee Falls, Splits, (unintelligible); it seemed like it was second nature to me.
As I said, just about everybody could dance.
What kind of a setup did you have in the band where you were playing the fiddle, did you tap dance with the tramp bands?

Well, you know, whoever could dance could with the tramp band. We'd play a tune, and maybe the next tune somebody would get out and dance. But we had what you would call a leader. He wasn't a leader who directed the band, but he was what we called a 'mugger' -- he'd get out in front and go through all kinds of wild antics, and like I say, being in a tramp band, we'd wear any kind of clothes, you know, just to look funny. And that was the times, you might say, they were the only clothes you could get.
Well, that was -- I was growing up, you might say, wearing those little tramp outfits with those singing groups.
Were you influenced by the music you heard on the radio in these bands -- say the broadcasts from the Three Deuces or the Grand Terrace?
In Chicago? Yes. Yes. Every night I would stay up late and when my mother told me to go to bed, I'd

turn on the radio -- they would broadcast from the Three Deuces, and I used to hear Jimmy Noone, I used to hear Tatum, I used to hear Roy Eldridge. And, I used to catch Fletcher Henderson's band from The Grand Terrace -- it was on 40th and South part of Grand then, listening to "Christopher Columbus", that was his theme song.

Naturally, Earl Hines -- that was his home base, you might say. And let me see, that goes to '36, '35, and then when Basie came through -- I'd catch all those broadcasts. And they had little taverns in the neighborhood and they'd have 2 and 3 piece bands in there, and somebody would have a piano -- just everybody seemed to be in to music.

We had a South Side Boy's Club I used to go over; Reverend Turner had a C Melody saxophone, and he had a baritone horn, and in Phillips Junior High, they were trying to start a band up -- they didn't have the instruments, so if you had an instrument, you were committed to join. So some of the days, I'm already playing the bass; I could play drums, but my fiddle was home made, I wouldn't take it to school, because we didn't have that kind of band -- it was a marching band.
So I took the C Melody and then I played the scale -- but I didn't like wind instruments -- never did.
Were you still playing in the church at this time, or had you completely gotten out of it?
Well, I didn't believe in mixing the two,

but by that time when I started with those older boys in the neighborhood, they come around and asked Ms. Turner could I go out with them, and I just kind of dropped out of the church. In fact, the church just seemed like it kind of disintegrated; I don't know what happened. But I didn't go back to the church.
What did Reverend Turner think of your playing with these bands?

Oh, he would say, 'That was a mess.' See, Reverend Turner was a strange musical man, and he had his beliefs. Now on Saturday nights, his favorite music movie was the 8th Street Theatre -- to me, that was a forerunner of this Grand Old Opry. Every Saturday night when I wasn't out hustling with the various new groups, he'd say, 'Now that's the kind of music you should listen to.' And I got a whole lot of the old Hoosier Hotshots; that's another side of it -- the music was beautiful. We had bands coming from the Black Hawk Restaurant down there in Chicago, Art Jarrett Gerard and I think Lawrence Welk used to broadcast. And later on, in the thirties, the Hotel Sherman, they were bringing big bands in.

Now I'm kind of getting ahead of myself - but there was just plenty of music around Chicago at the time in the thirties ... World's Fair; World's Fair of 1933 and World's Fair of 1934. I can remember when they opened up the taverns, Roosevelt come in and oh yes -- there was a tavern right across the street from where

we were living at the time -- 32nd and State. It would open up and one of the fellows come and got me, I guess because I was young and I could dance a little bit. We'd go in and one of them would play the piano. They had me tap dancing, they'd pass a hat, and if I made a quarter or a half dollar, I was doing good.

But I remember that period -- I'm going back -- this is 1933, just before Reverend Turner made that fiddle for me. The Vendome (phonetic) Theatre was still open, and Erskine Tate had a band in there, they used to have amateur shows -- and I wanted to get on that show so bad. I made it -- dancing. I didn't win anything cause I wasn't good enough, but the music, oh, I was crazy when I hit that stage. I don't know what routine I had; I forgot -- but the music was so beautiful.

Then another time, there was the Grand Theatre on the corner of 31st and State, and the Vendome was in the 31st block on State, and there was a little theatre called the Lincoln Theatre, and they would bring in stage shows. I remember my first movie -- of course Reverend Turner didn't know I was going. I went in, they had a stage show -- a vaudeville show -- and the movie was "City Lights" and the first talkie. Goodness, yes. The first talkie with Tom Tyler in some cowboy picture.
And I had never been to the movies; I didn't know -- nobody told me when to come out. I think I went in about 2 o'clock, and I stepped out of the show when it closed.
Was this the same time when Ruth Jones used to ask if you would go to the movies with her?
No, that was later. That was about 1936.
Was she singing then?
Yes she was, she was singing in church.
Oh, in church.
You know, but all in that neighborhood.
How did you cope with your studies with all this music? I mean, you were in school.

I was in school, and I don't know -- they knew that a few of us in the school was playing around, you know; we had a piano player, Horace Parnum, and I took my fiddle to school one day for assembly, and we played. That was just before I got out of grade school to go to Wendell Phillips. I would have little jobs, and Well, I would tell my teacher that I had to go and play -- this wasn't much later; I'd say about '38. No, it wasn't quite '38 -- '37. I was working with a band at that time. Mr. Robinson had a club called the Tuxedo Inn. Now he had seen me in the neighborhood by the taverns, you know, and he got the bandleader, a fellow named Buster Bennett -- got the bandleader to bring me in. He said, "Boy, I'm gonna buy you a fiddle. I want you to play in my club." Now they had a 5 piece band. Buster played alto and they had a trumpet player named Willie Jackson; we had a pianist named Martha Davis; she passed away. She I think, in her later years,

she had a duo -- Martha Davis Davidson and spouse -- a beautiful pianist. And, Mr. Robinson's son, Mundy -- he was the same age I was -- he played drums and I played the fiddle. Mr. Robinson bought me a fiddle -- I think he paid $75 for it, and he said every week, I'd have to pay him so much until I paid for it myself.

Well, we worked this club -- we had a regular show -- 6 girls in the line; 2 tap dancers, sometimes Butterbeans and Susie (unintelligible) would work the club. It was kind of a popular little club -- they had a lot of popular little clubs in Chicago then.

But that's when I got my first, real bass violin. I was still going to school, high school, junior high, and Buster got a record date for me. I'll never forget this. And I had to get permission from my teacher to make it, although I'm working every night. We worked from, say, about 9 or 10 o' clock at night until the owner said, Mr. Robinson said, "You could go home now." That means if there were 2 people left in the club, we have to play until they got ready to leave, and it might be daylight. I think I was making something like $3 a night -- or $2 a night.

And he was taking half of that for my fiddle. But I enjoyed it; I was getting a world of experience. And Buster had this record date for this guy named Melrose Mellow's, and I didn't realize who the fellow was -- Big Bill -- we made a

record called "WPA" and in later years I found out it was out of print. But I remember I played all that afternoon -- it was all blues, nothing but blues. Big Bill Broonzy. It was all blues dates. I don't know who the other blues guy -- they kept me on it, you know, I was what you might say the house bassist. I think I made $10, which was good money. I made only $10 a week.
But I was in junior high, and every night around 2 o'clock, Mr. Robinson would tell his son, Mundy, he would say, "All right, Mundy, you go on home. Wilbur, you play the rest of the show on drums."

So I had to switch from the bass to drums. I was still playing drums -- always did play drums as well as bass. So I played the rest of the show, and then when I go to school, that's when I started dropping out. I didn't go. I was still working.
Was Reverend Turner aware that you weren't going to school?

Well, he saw me, and I was working -- I was able to buy my own clothes and after all, he wasn't doing working on WPA, too well; he was underpaid, and so long as I was doing all right, I was not in no trouble. So if I didn't want to go to school, I didn't have to.
Well, in order to make this record date and playing in these clubs, you had to be playing professionally,
and you had to have acquired some technical ability.

Well, like I said, I would learn all the while -- I am still learning -- but during those times, the musicians who were around, they would help you. You know. Like, I said this Martha Davis -- when I first started playing with her, she would tell me, she would say, "All right, you're playing in B flat now, and you're playing in E flat, you're playing in D flat, playing in A flat." Well, I knew F,G and C. I knew those keys on my bass. But that was just a beginning. Buster would help me though.

Well, at the time, I was listening to a whole lot of music -- records -- almost in every neighborhood they had little penny vendors, little restaurants, you walked past, and you could hear all the music you want. Basie, Benny Goodman, Slam Stewart, Slim and Slam ... oh my God, so many good musicians -- naturally Duke was at the top.
Louis Armstrong?
Pops. Oh, boy, Chick Webb with Ella.
Chick Webb.

Oh ... there was a club, not a club, but a little place, a little dancehall -- like I said, I wasn't quite 14, and I was working in this club, and it was a little dancehall right down the 30th block on Cosgrove called The Vipers. Now, it was run by an old man they called Pop Pearson and his son, Charlie. Well, Charlie had -- to me, I

believe that was the first stereo -- he made a vendor, and played records -- he had about 6 or 7 loud speakers, and he built it, and he'd sit up there and work the controls, and he knew all the arrangements, these big bands, and certain bands he would turn it up, you know, turn the volume up, and oh, it was so beautiful -- it was just like being -- sitting up close to a big band.

And so I'm just listening -- that's when I first heard of "Jack the Bear" with Duke Ellington and Blanton. And so I knew a whole lot of the arrangements, and I knew a whole lot of tunes, just by listening. And the little 5 piece band I'm working with, we would play them -- "Jumping at the Woodside" and "One o'Clock Jump" -- even things the Ceford band was playing. Lanceford Luntzwood was very popular.
I've heard Eubie Blake and Earl Hines talk about learning music by listening, and how you have almost a photographic memory. All these tunes, it seems phenomenal, but that's how you learn.

You learn and you retain those tunes, you know? You never forget them. I mean, you might not play a tune for a year, but somebody will say, "Do you know so and so" - and he'll call the name; you can't remember the name, but as soon as he plays at least 3 or 4 bars, you know it and you can play it.
Well, that's how I came up -- I didn't have a musical

education -- but I learned by listening and doing. And like I said, when I left the Tuxedo Inn, I went down to -- the club just folded up; that was about '30 -- I went back to hustling with a group. Now, the group -- there was a guy by the name of Billy Milton, a guitarist, and little Lonnie Charles; he played guitar, and he had another guy named Bill who sang -- singing 4-part harmony, we had a cat out in front mugging. and he had another cat.

And like I said, we went back hustling to all the big nightclubs way up north in Chicago, not on the south side, because there wasn't much money out there, but all up Broadway; I remember the 5100 Club; you'd see Danny Thomas in there. And Lord Buckley -- Dick Buckley. They had shows, but they would let us in to come do a spot, and people would throw out coins, money on the floor. We'd make it like that.
We'd leave that club and go out -- we had a car, hire somebody out and we'd pass clubs in the neighborhood like that.
Was this the time when they were throwing the hot pennies?

Oh yes. We worked at, a place called Mannheim Road the Spanish Club out on Mannheim, I'll never forget -- that was our first spot, going out west of Cicero Avenue, to Mannheim Road, the Club Spanish -- this guy would always -- he loved to see us come in, and that's when we had the tramp band.
And one night, you know, they'd throw the pennies

out there, or the nickels and dimes -- the quarters or whatever, you know, while we were playing. And pretty soon the cats would jump out and say, "Yeah, man!" You know, let the people know you're enjoying it, so they'd throw the coins out there. And this guy, he had a streak of something in him, he told somebody to go in there and heat up this whole pan of change -- pennies, dimes, make them red hot and pull them out there, and the cat leaped out there. It ain't funny. He leaped out there, raking these coins in ... but that's what you had to do to earn a fair living; to be able to eat and buy you some clothes and what have you.
In the tradition of Fats Waller.

Well, that's what we used to call him after so many years -- progressive jeppin. Yeah, we didn't have to, but we did because it was something that you did. You might curse people who were calling you shine, or Roll your eyes whatnot, but that was the times. I don't know ... I look back on it, and it was still an education. And I learned -- I learned to play any kind of tune.

Of course, we'd run in to gypsy groups out there hustling -- Spanish groups, French groups, everybody -- anybody would be out. Ask if they could come in and play a few numbers, you know. pass the heat Sure, come on. And we had a good jam session one time with a troop -- violins and that -- couldn't speak a word of English but they were beautiful. And we'd go our way and they'd go theirs. We'd try not to run in to each other, but we had a regular route

around Chicago, and say, about three or four o'clock in the morning, we'd probably wind up out around the Club De Lisa -- that was an institution in Chicago -- at 5th and State. A wonderful drummer had a band there for years, and Red Saunders, and he had Eckstein singing in there. Really top notch acts used to come through there. Run by the De Lisa brothers.

But as a kid, like I said, music was all around Chicago. In every neighborhood, they had a band --- every little bar had one. At least they would have a band in there. See, three pieces playing "Jumping at the Woodside" "Every Tub" -- trumpet, drum and piano. And they would play. They'd almost play the whole arrangement, you know?
That's just the beginning though.
Were you taught music in any formal way by music teachers in school or anyplace else?

No. I had some -- there was a bass player named Truck Parham - saw me out on the street, you know, with my fiddle, he said, "Come by the house" -- and I went by his house one day; you know, I didn't have no money to pay him but he wanted to help me -- a young kid, you know -- and he showed me how he played double stops. Then there was another bassist out there, Henry Ford, and Taupus Dean, and a bassist named Walter Williams. I don't know what ever happened to him -- he used to give me strings whenever he'd see me, because I couldn't afford to buy a set, so he would give me some old strings and ....

Because I remember Erskine Tate was working down at one of those dance marathons -- what was the name of that club down on Wabash -- we'd stop by there and try to play; kind of spare the musicians a little bit -- a lot of people was dancing for these prizes. You know what I mean by a dance marathon? Dance for weeks.
For weeks?
Uh huh. Well, that band has got to play right along.
And this was in the thirties?
In the thirties, yes.
People would dance until they fell out.
Well, for a prize of $1,000 -- a thousand dollars was a whole lot of money. You know.
It sure was.
But like I said, there was a whole lot of music out there ... beautiful music.

Well, I was working down there with Buster Bennett like I said, at the old Tuxedo Inn, and it kind of closed, and I went back out hustling again with the fellows. And we wound up one night -- we went up to Harry James -- across the street from the Hotel Sherman, the Panther Room, and he was sitting in a little bar, and he come over and said, 'Come on in -- maybe you could join the tail end of the show and see what you can do.' And they had -- I'll never forget this --

Meade Lux Albert Ammons they had Meade Lux Lewis, Alan Edwards, Joe Turner, Pete Johnson, and the Harry James band, and Frank Sinatra was singing with them. And I don't know -- I hope I don't get in no trouble for saying it, but I met him, and we come back stage and the guys were saying just stand here, they were playing; they had just broadcasted -- they were broadcasting nightly -- and Sinatra was just talking to them; he said, "I'm Frank Sinatra" and he says "You hungry?" and I said, "Yeah" and he went back and bought me a sausage.

And after he came back from singing he says, "I'm gonna be a big star one of these days. This is my last week, and I'm going with Tommy Dorsey." And I was amazed that he'd even talk to me, you know. Like I said, I was just a kid, and being on the South Side, you didn't fraternize too much with the white people, you know.

I'll never forget it, though, he gave me a picture -- I lost that picture back in 1955; somebody stole my belongings, because I had messed up; if they didn't steal them then I left them there, never did find them misplaced them. But I moved out of this room, -- but I remember that; we went out that night, and oh my God, we played, we sang "The Lamp is Low" -- I'll never forget the routine we did. "The Lamp is Low" -- we did "The Sheik of Arabee" and we closed with "Tiger Rag" which we used as a flash, and we brought the house to their feet. And when we came backstage, whoever the manager was -- some guy named

Jerry was managing Harry James, and he said, 'Well, you got to sign these options. We're gonna take you out to Victor Hugo's out in the West Coast.' He says, 'We're gonna give you a couple of jobs playing up there -- at the Hotel Sherman -- for smokers.' However, we signed these options and we went down there a couple of times; they had a couple of jobs while the band was still there.

And when it was time for them to leave, he had to explain that he wouldn't accept no colored out at Victor Hugo's. But we were talented, and that group broke up right then. And somebody come by my house when I was staying with Reverend Turner and said, 'You want to go to Quincy, Illinois?' A trumpet player named Roy something -- I can't remember too well, but we went down there. Our piano player at that time was Bill Samual, with Roy's trumpet player, and alto player and a drummer, and myself -- and we had a girl singer. Her name was Toy Tori. We went down there ... a place called the Casino Blue Room in Quincy, Illinois -- right on the Mississippi River, across the river from Hannibal, Missouri.

And the job was for 4 months. And every little territory band at that time had somebody who did a show. I'd get out and dance, the piano player would do his number -- everybody had a little number to do. And I'll never forget it.
Anyway, I come back to Chicago after the job was

over, and I went to Detroit to play with some guys -- we went in the place of the Cats and Fiddles. The Cats and Fiddles had another gig, and they wanted us to play in their place as the Cats and Fiddles -- which we did. A place called the 12 Horsemen Club. Just for one night we played.

And I come back to Chicago and there was a telegram from a fellow named Flip Benson, this is 1939 -- and Flip had a 6 piece band, alto, tenor, trombone, bass, drum and piano. And Flip was what you would call a real musician; to me, everything they played was arranged -- he did the arranging. Flip is still alive now, I'm happy to say. I was in contact with him not too long ago, although I heard he just had a stroke, but the alto player, Charles Copeland is still alive out on the West Coast -- I've been in touch with him. But that's when I learned discipline.

We played nothing but the white clubs. I went back to Quincy with him because Bob Crist told him about me and that he needed a bass player, and he sent for me. I still got the telegram. I think my salary was to start was $21 or $22 a week, to start. And he gave me a raise periodically. And he treated me just like a son. See, that was in 1939. Yeah, the summer of 1939, and I went down and that's when I wore my first tuxedo. You know, I had been dressing in zoot suits and what not, but a tux, a dinner jacket, with black tuxedo pants -- and I thought I was something.
But Flip's band, we played nothing but beautiful

music. I think during that time, ASCAP and BMI -- we had a lineup from the club, and we broadcasted every night, and so we had to play all BMI tunes. Now my ear was sharp -- I could play anything I heard, you know, we'd rehearse, but I could play it. He tried to help me in every way; he would say, "You want to learn how to read? I'll teach you."

And I was wild, and a young cat, hanging with these grownups, and I thought I was something. I didn't have time. I could play, you know? And we were playing nothing but straight ahead music. We played every kind of tune imaginable.

But I stayed with that band from the summer of '39 up until the summer of '41 -- 6 months here, 4 months here, Quincy, Illinois; Springfield, Illinois; Grand Rapids, Michigan, and then back to Quincy. The last time I played Quincy with Flip, who comes in upstairs -- because the Casino Blue Room was a big rambling nightclub where they had the Blue Room downstairs and upstairs they had the big dancehall; they'd bring bands in there, and -- Kay Kaiser, his band with Ginny Simms -- all those kind of bands would come.

And I was just happy. And when we played Springfield, Illinois, this was during the period of the Springfield State Fair -- it was another state fair -- you used to see all kinds of bands out there. Some came out of St. Louis -- Louis Armstrong had a big band come through. T-Bone Walker come through with Les Hyte's big band ... oh, so many musicians. It
was jammed all day. Go all day and come back and jam all night. And then we went to Grand Rapids, Michigan -- but that's another story.
Did you have a set kind of show that you played with Flip's band?
Well, ...
Or did you play the drums in Flip's ...

No, I didn't play the drums in Flip's band. Every night, we had a little show we put on -- only if it was necessary though, if they called for it. But other than that, we just played dance music. And we'd do our little flash thing.
Flip and his band -- now these guys were older dudes and the younger cat beside me was Skeets -- he was the tenor player. Skeets was -- he had to be about 30 something, and I was 15.
Skeets Washley?

Skeets Washley was his name. He was out of Hannibal, Missouri. And Flip -- and Charles, our alto player, was out of Texas; his drummer was out of Kansas City, George Smith; Mitch Franklin was out from the southwest somewhere out there; he's still living, and Flip -- now, I can't remember exactly where Flip was from -- but they all come out of that Blue Devil's Band, you see; they worked -- and Flip told me he had worked with Walter Page Blue Devil's big band man, and they were on good
terms with Nat Towles -- those kind of bands out in the southwest, and they'd been traveling for years. You know, before I joined them.
Like I said, this was an education for me.
You got married and stayed in Grand Rapids.
Yes, I did.
And worked in a WPA band there. What kinds of things were you doing?

Well, we were playing -- this is 1941 -- the war had broken out, and so I got married, and Flip was going out to the west coast, and I didn't want to leave my wife, so some musicians around Grand Rapids said, "Well, maybe we can get you in one of the WPA bands here" -- so I put in for it, and they got me on.

What it was -- you go and play, you play at community centers, and I think Fort Custer had opened up, and we played there on Tuesdays and Fridays for the soldiers, you know, at the USO hall. Until our band just started -- the draft was grabbing them all; we had a big band, and they were grabbing the cats right and left. And I think it was in 1942, they dissolved it. Too many of them had to get in defense work.
Well, the fact that I was the father of 2 kids kind of kept me from getting in to the service quick, you know. So I left Grand Rapids and came back to Chicago, seeking work, and

I ran in to another fellow -- at least there was a fellow who come through there looking for me; they had heard about me - Jimmy Baker. He had a 6 piece band. And this was in '42. We went up to Mirinit and Minominee, Wisconsin, for a summer job, and it was a tenor, trumpet, bass, drums and piano, and I got a hold of an old friend of mine -- we used to hustle together in the tramp band days, Little Emmett Spicer, on guitar.

And so Emmett joined the band, come out of Wisconsin and we went to Fort Huron, Michigan, and we stayed on that job 9 months. I'll never forget that. It was the longest job. We only worked from 9 to a quarter to two, but it was so tedious, so monotonous. We played the same arrangements night after night, 7 nights a week and 2 matinees. One on Saturday and matinee one on Sunday. I thought I would go crazy.
One day I was so disgusted with playing that same stuff that I picked up my -- and I started to throw it out on the dancefloor but the guitarist stopped me, and kind of come to my senses.

But I stayed with that band up until the time Uncle Sam called. I was up in Monominee, Wisconsin in '43, when Uncle Sam sent me my draft papers. And I was accepted. So I joined Uncle Sam's Army Air Force in September, 1943.
You were 20 years old at that point.
That's right.
And what was your musical involvement in the army?

Well, when we went through our basic, we had 45 musicians and I didn't read, so I wasn't even apt to get in the army band or the post band or anything like that. But all these musicians -- they were just making up battalions; like I said, we were in the Army Air Force, and they made us engineers; half of us engineers. Combat engineers. However, you know, the rapport we had among the young cats; we were just happy to be together, you know, and we went through basic and we had the band -- as I said, 45 pieces.

And we were playing the marches for the battalion, and the battalion had almost 1,000 men, and after basic, we were getting ready to go overseas, so they sent down orders; they wanted us to make the base band -- we were down at Greenwood, South Carolina, and the colonel come and talked to us, and said if they pulled us out, it would stop this whole battalion from going.

And we didn't want to be a base band. I don't want to really get in to it, but I stayed in the service from '43 to January of '46. Overseas, down in the Pacific, went to Honolulu. From Honolulu to Guam, from Guam to Okinwa, Okinwa back to the states. So I met some good musicians during that period, and that's when I started in what they called the 'new music' -- what you'd call bebop. But it was beautiful. When I come out of the service, in '46, I started working around Chicago.
Now, I hadn't worked in Chicago since the thirties;
late thirties -- so it was a whole new ballgame for me.
But you had heard what they were calling 'new music' in the service.

Only at the end of my -- it was just before my discharge that I started hearing it, because we didn't hear it overseas. Not in Okinawa, anyway. I had heard a victory broadcast one night, but it wasn't reached over there. I didn't hear it until I got back to the States, and I just happened to hear a record. Of course, I heard Bird when he was with Jay McShann; he come through Chicago; I was on my way to Wisconsin, and I think they played, Jimmy McShann (Drum Boogie) Shannon's band played -- was it "Geron-Bogie" at the Regal Theatre. One of the two. I caught the band and I heard it.
I knew it was a new sound - a new sound, but nobody called it bebop.
What did they call it?
They didn't call it nothing. I wasn't really in to it because I had been in the service, you know.
Uh huh. But when you came back to Chicago, you worked with Stuff Smith?

Yeah, I worked with Stuff. But first, I worked back -- Buster was working at a place called Lips Lower Level, which turned out to be the Blue Note; one of the top nightclubs. But I came back to Chicago, and I'm working down there with a local guy, Innocent Smith and Little Ruth Crowder;
Little Sax Crowder had a four-piece group; a tenor, trumpet, bass and piano. And I'm working with them ...
No drums?

No drums. But Buster Bennett had a 4-piece band opposite us; they played 30 minutes and we played 30 minutes at this club -- the Lips Lower Level -- and what knocked me out, some old friends of mine, a piano player, and Israel Crosby Robert Montgomery and Jimmy [Bowlin] -- and that was another education; playing opposite that young man. I say 'young man' but playing and hearing all those beautiful notes he was putting out. With Buster and our band -- we would come close, you know, exchanging ideas.

And then somebody around the corner told Stuff Smith he needed a bass player; he was going to a club out at North Side. And so I worked for Stuff for 2 weeks. Then after Stuff, the next name I worked with was Roy Eldridge and Sonny Stitt.
Sonny Stitt was in the band?

Yeah, well, see, Roy come to Chicago looking for a band, and he knew Stitt was hanging around, because I think that's where Eckstein's band broke up was in Chicago; in fact, they did break up in Chicago. They played the Regal Theatre and that was the end of it. But Stitt was around then, and he told me one night, it was at a little after hours place, all the musicians used to come and jam,

called 'Slappy's' on 29th and Indiana. And after I got off my job downtown on Sunday, I'd pull by there. You know, and we just jammed all morning, to at least 1 or 2 o'clock in the afternoon. And Stitt would be down there, and he says to me, 'Man, I got a job for you if you want it.' He had [Don Rail] Anderson drumming, a pianist named Willie Jones, who, Willie incidentally, was playing that locked-hand style, and still is, Big Willie Jones -- he said you're going to work with Roy Eldridge. Elton: Roy had 2 weeks up in Milwaukee, and he asked me did I want it, and I said, 'Yeah.'
So we bought uniform jackets at least, and we went to Milwaukee with Roy Elton.
What kind of things were you playing?

Oh, we were playing beautiful things. We were playing music, and Stitt was playing -- you might say we were young turks, and we were able to play any kind of music, but we added on what they would call 'bebop' if you want to call it that. Right down the street, Charlie Ventura had his band, and had this vocalist Buddy Stewart with him, Kai Winding, Shelly Manne -- I think Buddy Clark was on bass, and we were doing pretty good. During that time, this pianist, Heywood, was in town, playing music up in Milwaukee, you know.
So after that gig, we got to know a few people, and I started working around Chicago with local groups, and I'd
run into Ike Day and Vernel Fournier and so many beautiful musicians.
Everybody that had lived in Chicago, or seems, almost passed through Chicago, knows something about Ike Day. He's become almost a legend. Tell us about him.

He was a legend. Every drummer that ever came to Chicago would find Ike. Ike had his problems, but he was young and phenomenal. He was upsetting. That was during the days when, like I said, Red Saunders was one of the top drummers out there in Chicago. But the Delisa Club would have on Monday mornings would have a breakfast dance, after the last show at 4 o'clock. The breakfast dance started about five.

Ike might come in there and Red would let him sit in, and they had this great big, hydraulic stage and Red had maybe about 15 pieces up there. And Ike'd come up there and start soloing, and then -- they had those little wooden beaters, and people would beat along with the music, but they wouldn't beat along with Ike when he was playing drums. You could hear a pin drop when he was soloing, he was so beautiful.

Any drummer in the country -- and I'm talking about from old man Joe Jones -- everybody that ever come through Chicago -- and run across Ike, they had a world of respect for that young man. He just wouldn't leave. He had a chance one time, I never will forget, I guess this was in '48 or '49 when Woody Herman was at the old Blue Note, and Ike was hanging out with somebody. And he

went down there, and they let Shelly Manne-- Shelly Manne let him sit in, and of course, Shelly was cutting out from the band; there was Shelly, and Oscar Pettiford on bass, and Gene Ammons was there; (unintelligible) -- that was the band that played More Moon, I think it was, one of those Herds. And Ike played there.

And so Shelly said, "I'm leaving and Woody'd really like to hire you." So as I understand it, Ike didn't have a pot -- didn't have a set of drums; which he never did -- somebody was always buying him some. But his lifestyle was such that he couldn't hold on to anything -- a whole lot of us went through that. However, he wanted to know how much he was paying -- and Ike had asked Shelly how much, and he said, "Well, I'm getting $450 a week." And Willie said, "I'll pay you $350" and Ike said, "No, I can't work for that." And he didn't. I think Ike had borrowed a shirt that night from somebody just to be clean.

But there were so many cats like that in the country, or used to be, you might say. Now, it looks like the youngsters, are fortunate enough, their parents prepared them -- they buy them the best instruments and what not.
But even then, some people seemed to have had more than others. Like Wilbur Campbell likes to tell the story about Ike Day.
Oh yes. Wilbur said he went in and sat in and he'd been practicing; he just knew he was ready to play with the group. And he said he went down to this place called

The Ritz, and there was a tenor player around called that Dave Young had -- I think he had a sextet then -- a popular place -- and Wilbur said he'd sit in, and Dave turned around and said, and screamed, he said, "Ike, come up here and play some time." And Wilbur said he was so mad he'd get up off the drums and go home and practiced.

Well, Ike was like that -- he'd show you anything. He showed me a whole lot of things. He showed me how to play shows. Ike -- I think he lived out in Harvey, so that was close to Calumet City where they had all these strip joints, you know, like in Vegas -- and these dancers and what not would strip. Strip had come in with big band arrangements. They might have 4 pieces out there, or they might have 5, some only 3, but they got 16 pieces arrangements, and they let you play. Ike was in demand out there like mad.
He was playing all those kinds of music?

He'd play everything. The man was a genius. There's no drummer, I think, in the country that came to Chicago and never met Ike or heard of him. I'll tell you, I mean, all of them -- Klook, old man Max, Joe Jones ...
So in addition to being -- to keeping time, as you would say, he was ...
He was all over. The man was phenomenal. He was something.
Who were some of the other people that

Gene Ammons was around -- he came back; that was his home. And these cats were just starting ... look, everybody had money in those days, '46 and '47, and like I said, every neighborhood had a little club, had 4 pieces, and musicians were coming out of the woodwork; in fact, they were working -- but it all had to do with tenor saxophone -- trumpet players didn't have too much work, you know, but saxophones had it.
(Interruption)

Lester Young, the big bands had broke up, you might say; they didn't have too much work, and the leading bars for a combo was a saxophone, and everybody was playing tenors, even -- there were no alto players out there, because Bird seemed to have wiped them off the face of the earth. Really, everybody wanted to play tenor, and some of them were using the technique that Bird was using on the tenors, but that was -- everybody wanted to hear a tenor saxophone -- just everyone.
Do you think people were intimidated by the things that Bird was doing?
The musicians?
Right.
Well, I say, like the altos I knew just got out of the service, they switched over to bass. And he

says the reason he switched over to bass, how can he play like that -- and a whole lot of altos had put their horns down because of it. Not really, but they would say, well, what's the use? Everybody expects you to sound like Bird Berg, and if you did, you were copying.

Now there was a whole lot of musicians who hate to copy, you know, the creative musicians. I mean, that wasn't it. Just like, me, speaking about myself, now I loved Blanton, I loved him, and I took a little bit from Blanton, took a little bit from Israel Crosby and I put a little bit of Wilbur Ware in there, so I believe I got my own little way of playing, you know? So that's me. I don't find, like I hear people come up, saying, "You don't sound like so and so and so and so .." and I say, "Yeah, I have to sound like me."

I had a good friend of mine, a young bassist -- a Malachi Favors, with the Chicago Art Ensemble, and Maul brilliant young bassist, younger than I am Wilbur and he used to come for me every morning, and say, "Let's just play something for me." He stayed maybe 2 or 3 blocks from where I was living in Chicago during that time, '48, and I played and he was learning. You know, I'd show him what I knew, and now like I say, technically, I didn't know too much, but playing around -- Israel was showing how to hold my hand correct, you know, and I was watching people that was holding their hands correct.
I went to teach him -- this is when I got myself

kind of messed up, but I wanted to make some money -- not make some money, but go to school on the GI Bill, I had that option, and I went down and I took the test. I passed. The lady seemed to be surprised that I passed the test. She said, 'Well, you passed every one of them' -- you know. But hey, I had been hearing sounds all my life.
A music test?

Yeah, a music test, you know. Is this note a flat or is that a sharp? You know? Well, I say, well, I want to study bass. Now I was afraid to learn how to read music, simply because I had a mental block about it. I'll go back some years when I was working down there at that club on 31st -- the Tuxedo Inn -- working with Buster Bennett and his band.
Martha Davis?

Martha Davis, yeah. An alto player came through there out of St. Louis named Burt Brazier. Now Burt come through Chicago with a pianist -- only had one leg, Greer? and a drummer was named Sonny Greer; they were all out of St. Louis. Swinging little cats. And I mean they were older than I was. I was just, like I said, just a teenager. And they were playing, oh, to me -- Burt was sounding like Benny Carter would sound, you know, on alto. But he didn't know the music. I didn't find this out until later, because I had run in to him up in Grand Rapids, Michigan when I joined

the WPA band -- he was in the WPA band. He remembered me. And I said, 'Burt?' And he said, 'Bubble ...' -- he used to call everybody 'Bubble Kitchen'. He said, 'Bubble Kitchen, I never learned how to read music. I can hardly play it unless it's written out.' And I took that advice and I figured if I learned how to read, I would lose all my natural ability.

That was just ignorance on my part, you know. But through the years, I was afraid, you know. I could play -- anything I hear I could play, and I can anticipate. It's funny, but I've always been able to do that. I made recordings with people -- spontaneous. We'd play and I know exactly what he's gonna do, you know.

And to me, that's a gift. And maybe I was lazy, which I guess, I was. I went to school -- my father was teaching there in downtown Chicago -- and I went down on the GI Bill -- I only had to go one hour a week, and you know, I couldn't even make that? And he thought I was phenomenal -- he said, 'How could you play so when you never studied?' And I mean, he liked me; he would have helped me tremendously, but I had hooked up in to something else, which was against everything, so I stopped going. And I figure that everything I've done through the years has been for the best, or that it was the way it was supposed to be.
So I don't have no -- if I were to go back and do it, I'd do the same things that I did, you know, but it's all
alike ... it was beautiful.
Who were some of the other people that you played with at this time besides Ike Day and [Dorel] Anderson? Did you play with Wilbur Rubin Campbell at this time, Nicky Hill?

Oh, well, Nicky Hill come up a little later. Nicky Hill and Wilbur -- I guess Wilbur was playing around -- but I was working club dates -- and oh yeah, going back to this, I worked up at a place called the Argyle Show Lounge, up on the North Side. There was a tenor player named Gypsy -- a white tenor player. He loved Pres -- he played just like him. When I met Lee Konitz -- and oh, that piano player out of Chicago -- a whole lot of white Chicago musicians; I started getting gigs over there with these guys, you know, and I got to know a whole lot of them -- the white cats.

And they'd come on the South Side jam sessions, you know, and so I started getting jobs over there -- and oh, I had all kind of little gigs -- a gig here and a gig there. Different people. Chris Anderson Henderson, Van Vaughn Freeman ... the Freeman brothers; Van Buzz Buzz and George, and a piano player named Jo Jo Parnell.
Were you playing with Chris at this time?
Yeah. Chris and I, we played many gigs together. Little blind pianist -- brilliant, brilliant pianist.
People don't know about Chris Anderson Henderson.

Not really. You know, I was a shy dude; I was afraid of the big name stars, and they come through, I was just afraid to be around them. I remember I went to a session one morning down at a place called the Mocambo -- it was a real swinging street; 39th and Cottage Grove in Chicago. And they had clubs back to back and everybody was having Monday morning jam sessions then. And that would go on all morning and all day, up until late at night.

However, this particular morning, I would come in the club, the Mocambo, a little bar, it was owned by Leonard and Phil Chess, who later had the Chess recording company -- and I used to work Monday nights there.

But anyway, I go in there and it's morning -- with and Malachi and a couple of the guys we were hanging out with, and the bandstand was kind of full -- and Flip the trumpet player, we went to school together -- he was working with Red Saunders' band at the time -- he's up jamming, and he says, "C'mon, come up on stage; come up and play" -- you know. So the bass player gave up the fiddle and I end up playing, and we had a good groove going on, and I noticed they pushed me out in front, you know? Go solo. I'm Not much of a solo, but I do what I want to do. And I don't realize that Oscar Pettiford is in the house. He's sitting across -- I'm behind the bar playing, you know, with the cats -- and they tell me that when

I started playing, Pettiford had been sitting up there with his head down on the table, you know, between some other musicians, and when I started playing, he raised his head up and started listening.

So when I finished playing, I was getting ready to come down, the trumpet player, Flip, said, "Did you know that Oscar Pettiford is in the house?" -- and I felt like going through the floor; I had that much respect for the man, you know. And I'm trying to get out from under the bar, behind the bar, you know, coming out and Pettiford was coming in to meet me. He says, "Hey, wait a minute; hold it -- what's your name?"

I told him my name, and I'm stuttering -- not knowing what to say. He says, "I want you to come back to the hotel tomorrow." He was in town with Louis Bellson up on the North Side, and I said, "Okay" -- but I wasn't about to go. As a matter of fact, I said we're going in the morning. I said, oh man, you know.

Anyway, the next morning, he was at my house at 9 o'clock, and he said, "Man, we're going to see Pettiford" -- and I said, "Oh, man, I got to go somewhere else and do this." And he said, "No, we're going up there." And I did go -- went by there. He got up and he showed me, he says, "Wilbur, I like your bass playing, man." I mean, it was real beautiful just to talk to him, and he showed me -- he got out a cello and he says "I'm gonna amplify this and I'm gonna play it." So when

I first met him -- you know, that cat was beautiful. There he is when I come to New York, I didn't have a fiddle but he gave me one of his fiddles -- that's before he went to Europe. Oh, that's a long story. But that was one of the people that I met, you know.

Like I say, I was kind of shy in meeting the big names. Those fellows would come in and they'd walk in the club, and they'd kind of look down their noses at you. They don't know you -- you don't have no big name; they looked down their noses at you, you know. And actually, most of the Chicago musicians seemed like they were just waiting. They'd say, "Okay, you kind of snubbing me, huh?" But then they'd get up there and play, and then they would win the respect of the man, you know.

That happened many times. Some people used to call them cutting sessions (UNINTELLIGIBLE) -- they didn't know what it was about; they were just showing the person; saying, well, you're in my hometown; you know, you got to give me a little respect, too.

I appreciate you and I admire you -- you know, and you knock me out, but I got a little something to say, and they would say listen to this -- a lot of musicians, when they came through Chicago, they had to come, as we say, fully dressed.
Right.
They had somebody in Chicago for everybody, and so ...
You were in '50-51, you switched back to
drums. How did that happen?
Yeah. Well, I got in to the wrong lifestyle, and at the time I had 2 instruments, and I lost them.
Was one of those instruments the one that Mr. Robinson bought?
Oh no. That fiddle, I lost that fiddle when I went in the service.
Oh ...

I sold that fiddle to somebody, you know. When I come out of the service, I bought a fiddle from Israel, and I went down and bought another one, so I had 2. But then, after I started working on it for awhile, and got curious about something that I had no business getting curious about, I ...

Well, that's an area, too, that should be talked about. A lot of people try to dismiss that -- we were reading a story called 'Will the Circle Be Unbroken?' and it was, in a sense, it showed that that is a part of the black community, even though the black community doesn't manufacture it or import it or anything like that. That's where it is, and in this particular story, it was about a black musician, and Henry Dumas saw -- it was called 'Will the Circle Be Unbroken?' -- he saw dope as being closer to the circle than people at times. Just like Wilbur Campbell was saying that they didn't want you to start, but they couldn't stop, either,

because they couldn't stop themselves. In other words, what I'm saying is that it has nothing to do with music, but it did have something to do with the community, with the environment, relating to ...

Relating to the different cats. And that's true. Like, I was kind of running around what you would say -- I'm trying to get in with the hip crowd. I was in already, but I didn't feel like I was really in. They were hiding this dope and stuff from me, and I wanted to know what the hell it was -- I was curious. But they say curiosity killed the cat.
But young people are doing that now.
Young people do do it now.

With different things -- it was I guess, sort of mystical, sort of mysterious, as long as it was in the black community. Now it affects so many people in so many different ways -- we did the same thing, for instance, with alcohol. You hadn't grown up until you smoked a cigarette and had a drink. Well, you had the same thing.

Same thing. When I first went to Quincy, Illinois, with the band -- not Flip's band, but this other band, Roy, I hadn't -- I mean, I would drink a little wine with the gang, because there were 10 of us on one pint, you know, and we'd swear we were high. But when I got to Quincy, they were serving it in these little pitchers -- whiskey -- and I didn't know nothing about drinking whiskey;

I was just sipping wine. So when we got upstairs, one of the guys says, "Do you drink?" "Yeah" -- I mean, I'm trying to be a man, and I wasn't but 15. "Okay, here, take a drink." And it was this little small pitcher; and he was pouring me a shot -- I picked up the pitcher and drank the whole pitcher.

He looked at me ... and I'm thinking I'd done something big -- I'm grown, you know? He said, "I bet you won't do that again." And I ... he said, "I'll buy a load." -- I think it cost something like 50¢ or 35¢, something like that -- and I threw that down.

And he looked at me ... but he didn't tell me, see, you weren't supposed to drink like that. But he said, "You gonna learn it" -- and actually, I did. I got up from the table; we were getting ready to go. The last thing I remember when I opened that door to go, and the next thing I knew, I fell right flat on my face. And naturally I was sick, oh, all that morning, and I'm sick and cold and all, and I'm just getting down and gagging.

But did you think that stopped me? No. I had to play it straight out. I didn't think nothing was smart about it; I didn't look at it like that. As far as the dope was concerned, I just didn't want to get sick. I didn't really enjoy what they called the high, because I didn't know -- I was asleep. I had a little gig with some guys when I first started messing around. I said, "Oh, I won't get hooked. Not
me. I'm too smart for that." That's what I'm thinking now.
Uh huh.

And I'm working every night, right in the midst of it, and the guys would come back and say, "Hey, take a little snort of this" -- he said, "You won't get a habit" -- so I snorted it, and went back up on the bandstand, and the drummer was the leader of the band -- a little cat named Bill Pinkert, and he said, "Wilbur, wake up." I would say, "What do you mean, wake up?" You know, I had 2 fiddles, I had a bank account -- I didn't have to take this guff from this guy. Besides, he wasn't really caring if I played the drums or not, but he had the job in the band.

And he kept doing it. I said, "Man, get you another bass player." And he said, "Wait a minute. We can sit down and talk about this." Oh, we were just smashed, and we were changing our uniform every intermission, and working steady. I said, "Now, don't tell me I'm sleeping on the bandstand. I don't want to work here no way." And all the guys in the band would say -- just 4 pieces -- would say I was nodding. "Me? I never nod." I didn't know. I didn't know what effect it had. I've seen the junkies out there, but I didn't associate that with me. No, not me.
So it wasn't long, I was right back out there with them. And I lost my fiddles. And a guy offered me a job playing drums. So I went out to Calumet City.
The strip joints?

The strip joints . See, everybody at one time worked out there. Vernell was working down the street, Ike had in fact, he showed me how to play one lady's act -- a lady called Tanalia -- she worked with snakes -- a mystic type thing, alligator -- we had 5 pieces out there. And the guy that had the bag was called Jive Jackson, a trumpet player -- bless his soul. Jive had the bag. He didn't have nothing but junkies in his band, all except the tenor player -- he didn't fool around.

But the piano player, myself, Jive -- well, he was the leader; he had the bag. Now, he was selling pills and would give us each 2 pills before we go to work and 2 pills when we got off work, and made sure he paid our rent -- we didn't have no pocket change to buy some cigarettes or anything -- and we were happy.
We worked from 9 until daylight. And Jive was making all the money. We didn't question it, so long as he kept our habits up, you know. And had a roof over our head.

Well, I did that up until about 1950 -- that was about a year -- '49-50 was my hardest time, and the guy offered me a job with Billie Holiday -- a little club on the north side; a trio -- she had a piano player, Carl Drinkard, and yeah, I want to make it. We got a drummer out of Chicago -- a beautiful drummer, a white dude named Guy Devereaux -- he loved Ike Day and played just like him, and I don't know whether he thought he
thought he was supposed to play with sticks behind Billy, but he did ...
What were they?

She said, 'No sticks ... brushes.' Wam, Wam, she Naturally, wouldn't fired me and him. Now she had to get rid of the piano player. But that was the first time I worked with her. And then I had to pay my dues. Drugs caused me to go to the House of Correction in Chicago, and I spent all of 1952 in there.

When I came out, I was clean -- '53, Ike Morris Hyte has just preceeded me, he left -- that was just before he died. I was in there, he carved up some sticks and sent them down to my cell and he said to keep practicing, you know, keep your wrists up, and I did. And when I come out, I got a job at a place called the Flame -- that was on Oakwood Blav., working and a trumpet player -- a trumpet and violinist -- Melvin Porter Kilbert, Moore and alto was Killman, Earl Phillips was on drums, and Jimmy Boyle was playing piano. And we were working at a place called the Flame, and Jo Jo Joe Adams was a blues singer, and all the blues singers used to come through there -- in fact, any singer would come there -- Joe Williams, Della Reese, Betty 'Bebop' Benny Carter, and ... the fellow who wrote 'Two Years of Torture' -- oh God, a beautiful cat, Jimmy Witherspoon used to come, too. Oh, it was beautiful.
And after '53, Johnny Griffin come out of the service, and we had a job down at the Bludnote. I was with

Ella -- it was Johnny Griffin, and Babs, Wilbur Campbell Camel, George Freeman, and I forgot this kid's name -- I got it down on an old picture, if I can't get to it, but he's out on he coast; he's been working with an arranger -- a pianist, he's from Chicago; he's been working with Super Sax -- lives on the West Coast. (Lou Levy - ed.)
However, Ella was working with Shadow Wilson; Jimmy Wood on bass, a trio -- and John Lewis was playing piano. They were the four -- the Maldez Quartet. She'd work 30 minutes, we'd work 30 minutes.
Did Joe Joe have his show?

Well, what he called his Joe Joe Show, he'd have these little singers with him, and we played blues, shuffle blues arrangements, and they had people like Della Reese come in, Betty "Bebop" Bee-Bop Carter, two girls - all singers, you know, and that would be the show. That was in '53 on over gigging around different theaters, working with Eddie Chamblee to the winter -- something happened between there and John Young.

Then in '54, at the same time Ike Day died, I think that was in '54 when he passed away. In fact, that was when the doctor told him he had TB and told him if he didn't stop playing, it would kill him, and Ike said, "Well, I been playing all my life and that's the way I'm gonna die." And he almost did. It got so he would get on a bandstand, and on one session, you'd get him playing and his feet would swell up so bad, we'd have to help him up off the drums.
But there was a new era coming and all that next

year in '54 -- that was when Johnny Griffin, Clean Head, Junior Mance, Jimmy Matz, Buddy Smith and myself were working for this same guy at the Flame; he had 2 clubs. The Flame and Basin Street -- right there in Chicago. And oh boy, we used to have swinging times. Tune Up, Clean Head's tune; Johnny Griffin playing his butt off -- I remember seeing Stan Colemang Hawkins and Ben Webster in the club one night -- that was an experience.
them, I didn't talk to him. Like I said, I was always shy with those big names.
Did that band ever make a record?

The band? Yes, it did. Only Clean Head wasn't on it. This was the band, you know, with Buddy Smith and Junior Mance and myself and Griff -- they had a disc jockey in Chicago, oh, he was very popular at that time. Al Benson. He come by the club and told Griff Red he wanted us to record. For him.

And so we said okay, and we go by the next day -- we go by Al's house, he had a home over on the South Side, in his basement, and he says he had a couple of tunes he's gonna fix. Al paid us off -- they made about $50 a piece -- and we recorded the next day after we rehearsed it, and I think they released that about '56 or '57 -- I think Al Benson had a tie up with the Chess Brothers, and I think it came out on Chess Records or Veejay -- I don't know which one -- but it was called "JG", and ...
This is Argoy LP 624.
Yeah, well, it was all souped up -- Chess or Argoyte or Veejay, I don't know which one, but....
The Chess Producing Corporation.

Yeah. Well, that's the date we did. That was about in the winter of '54, I know, when we did that, because, see, I stayed with the man -- in fact, we had one of the swingingest bands on the South Side; we were working; this guy Ellsworth Ellis, Mason has the Flame down in Oakwood, as well as the Basin Street out there on 63rd and Cottage.

And we worked, maybe, a week out there -- then we replaced the band that he had down there at his other club. Dr. Joe Joe Adams had a little show, down at the Flame, and a cat named Benny Kelly -- a comedian -- had a show out there at Basin Street. And our show -- we had Clean Head singing with us, as well as Flynn, featuring the 4 pieces -- they had a thing where Cleanhead they played the opening tune with us on alto, but Griffin did most of the solo.
We did this record date, and it came out real nice. I think it's out of print now, though.
Do you want to talk about that date?
Segal wrote the liner notes. Joe, Seegle ...
Yeah, Joe was in on it -- quite a few of the names out there.
Well, he says he went back with Johnny Griffin from his teenage years.
It's possible ... it's possible.
Since he was 15 years old.

Joe's been on top of the music scene in Chicago for years, you know; like -- see, Chicago was kind of split up. There was the north side, west side, and the south side. You don't really have no east side; it's east now, but all the real, I would say, swinging stuff was out the south side and maybe further north. Got around Argyle then, you know -- Lawrence Avenue, white clubs and what not.

Then on the west side of Chicago, you had all the and Howling Wolf blues joints. That's where Muddy Waters, and all those kind of people -- Blind John, all those people; Willie Dixon, they had that territory. And you would go and play a gig on the west side, and people wouldn't accept you -- there were a few diehard jazz lovers, but if you weren't playing the harmonica, Spitoon Blues, you was in trouble.

I got to tell you this, though ... this happened, I think before Sonny Rollins -- this happened in '55, after I left Griffin. The little guitar player I was raised up with out in Chicago, Leo Blevins, a little short dude -- he would come and stay right on top of everybody that played. And he didn't fool around or nothing like that, but he was in your corner, and he knew who to get -- he could play himself; he had a brother played piano named Bobby -- but Leo come and

got Sonny Rollins, who was out there then -- that's where he joined Max to return back east, and he says, "I got a gig." He hired Sonny, himself on guitar, Chris Henderson on piano, Wilbur Campbell on drums. He said, "Man, we got to go on the West Side and play this gig." And he would say, "We got to play blues now." And that means fast blues, slow blues, shuffle blues -- that's all they want to hear.

Okay, a gig is a gig. I think we made $10 a night. But it was worth it. We'd go over there, and oh, we thought we were playing some blues. We got funky -- Leo even fell on his knees; he could do that ... fell on his knees bending them strings, you know; something like T-Bone Walker would do, and when we finished playing the blues, we thought we really had gotten to the people, and some guy way in the back of the club hollered, "All right now, why don't you play some blues!" And he had taken all of the starch out of us.
I guess so.

But that was the times. Those places were something. I mean when you go to the West Side to play a gig, you knew you were going over there to play the blues. You know, you could play all the way out changes you wanted, but it didn't phase nobody.
This was the first time you recorded 'Riff Raff' on the JG album, right?
Yeah, uh huh.

That was your tune. And in the liner notes, when Joe Segal is talking about it, he says that this is reminiscent of (unintelligible) and then he talks about how these are the examples; why you were called the "Monk of the bass days" on this tune, Riff Raff.

Riff Raff? I can't see that. I don't believe that ... I don't know what he means by that. Riff Raff was just one of my ideas, and we run it over. And that was it. I had something to do with somebody else, I believe, in later years. After I played with him. But Leon Blevins had a part in that.

Well it could be then, I don't know how he means that, either, because he says that the flavor of the great Thelonious Monk permeates the proceedings of Riff Raff, and was most reminiscent of (inaudible) Well, You Needn't;"
Well, maybe he's talking in terms of the same kind of feel, you might say.
I suppose so.
(CUT)
Would you talk a little bit about the time immediately preceeding your departure from Chicago to New York?
Well, that was '56. The Jazz Messengers

had been in town -- I didn't catch the first, the original, group -- that was the one with Horace Mobley Donald and Hank Moby, Don Byrd, Doug Watkins, and Art Blakey Reckie -- That's the original Messengers they were the originals. They had been in, and I missed the band, and Max was working at the Beehive, and I had met Max before --back in the forties -- when he was with Bird Byrd, so Little Leo Blevins got me one night -- late one night, and said, "C'mon, Willie, let's go out and catch Max. -- -- " play some nights."

I had heard about Clifford Brown, had never met him -- and Malachi told me they were in the band down at Morris Brown College -- and Clifford had his first automobile accident in that college band, and spoke about it. I had heard what a great trumpet player he was, and I had hardly heard the band -- I didn't have access to no records, or recordings of the Max Roach Quintet: Clifford and Harold Land and Richie Powell and George Morrow. So I said, "Okay Leo" -- Leo wanted to get over to the club and all that ... and so I went with him, and we went by the Beehive, and I guess we got there just before the last set, and the crowd was kind of thinned out and Max was off the stand, and Leo introduced me to him, and Brownie.
Leo knew him already then?

Yeah, Leo -- see, he was on top of everybody. Like Dexter used to stay at his house, and the late Rahsaan Roland Kirk used to stay at his house also. Well, Leo was like that -- he was the type of cat who played with
quite a few of them, and was always ready for a jam session. He was a go-getter.
Yeah?

However, so we were standing there by the band -- and they got up on the stand, and Leo said, "Why don't you let Wilbur sit in?" You know, he didn't tell me he wanted me, or that he was going to ask that, you know, so he said, "C'mon!" So he knew that Leo wouldn't say that if I couldn't play, so I asked George Morrow, and he said, "Uh huh, c'mon."

And so naturally, I don't know whether they had ever heard me, but you know, they liked to try you ... see, if you had the nerve to get up there and play, you had better be prepared to play. And right away, he called Cherokee, with the tempo very fast -- and oh, I felt so good, playing with these giants. And we went in to it. They were only playing for 30 minutes ... and we played 30 minutes.
Of Cherokee?

Cherokee, yeah. (Unintelligible) Brownie, and Max, A.. just beautiful. And when we finished, Max got up with the microphone in his hand, and he went to say, "Ladies and gentlemen ..." -- and the owner of the club, Sol Tenenbaum, announced over the other mike, and this was Monday and Tuesday, which was the off nights; the club was running 7 nights a week with the regular group running from Tuesday until -- no,

from Wednesday until Sunday, and the alternate night trio or whatever, Monday and Tuesday. So he has the microphone and he is about to announce, you know, and Sol Tenenbaum says, "This Monday and Tuesday, the Wilbur Ware Trio!" And Max looked around and said, "You done played me up on my gig."
And this was such a surprise --and a joyful one for me, and at the time, Jody was in the audience.
Jody Pritcher?

Yes. He had just got his discharge from the service, so he comes and he says, "Who do you have on the piano, Wilbur?" And I said, "Jodie, you can have it." And I was thinking in the back of my mind that we could make it. So I started that month ... so I would go on Monday and Tuesdays down there, but that was (unintelligible) and George and Brownie ... Brownie said, "Man, I like your playing; come on by the hotel." Well, naturally George Morrow and I hung out -- bass players, and I contacted Wilbur, and we played the Monday and Tuesdays.
The next group to come in -- well, it wasn't a group so what Sol was doing, we were working the off nights, the trio -- rhythm section; piano, bass and drum, and here comes Themonius.
When?
That following Wednesday, that following week. And Sol said, "Well, you know, you're the house rhythm section" -- so that meant we had to play behind Thelonious.
So, Jody was off, so they all said, "Well, who are we gonna get?" So Wilbur Wilt said, "Well, let's get Griffin." And I said, "Good idea!" the following week So I remember Griff came in ...
A quartet!

Quartet. And that was my introduction to Thelonious, and with five of us Wilbur and I why, we'd hang out all during the week. And he said, "How come I never saw you when I came to Chicago?" Well, what could I tell him? This is Thelonious, the first time I ever meet the guy, and I'm standing in awe of this giant. But he was a beautiful person, you know? And I remember that well, because at the end of the week, he received a telegram from his wife saying his mother died, and wanted him to come home right away.

He says, "Well, "I left New York when mama was alive and I don't want to go back and see her in the casket and all that ..." because Sol had asked him to stay over an extra 2 nights to work with us, which he did. And the following week, here come -- we played behind Art Farmer -- Jody, and we hired little John Jenkins on alto, you know, and that went on - and anyway, I fooled around, and I didn't show up -- Drugs had something to do with that.
Well, how long did you keep that gig there?
I stayed there maybe a couple of months.
Uh huh.

Then I went out of town with Leo. We went down to Rock Island for a week -- one of them little joints down there. And I came back in town, and I had a gig with Ira Sullivan Art Solomon, somewhere -- I forgot where, and he said, Blakey "Well, man, Art Baker just come back in town." So I said, "Well, I got to catch that band, you know."
