So we go out the Stage Door -- a place called the Stage Door Lounge; 63rd and Blackistone. These were all nightclubs, and I had a chance to listen to the great Lou Buhaina Ayman -- that was a beautiful man.
Was he playing Buhaina then?

Oh yeah, for a long time, but he was Buhaina you know, he was still Art Blakey; that was his Muslim name. I think the band all gave their notice, I'm not sure. Anyway, he asked Ira and I to come up and sit in, and we did -- so he taught us our names for future reference, and not long after that, I'm hanging out -- Ira and I went down to Hannibal, and Wilbur Campbell and Eddie Baker Missouri, and play a little weekend gig, and when I come back, we were all hanging out around the Cotton Club -- that was the swinging joint -- something like the Flame used to be -- a Monday morning, Monday night all day jam session, you know? And it was run by 2 musicians -- Bobby Paine, and I forgot the other pianist.
And it was something like a [clan] house of musicians. See, I didn't have no permanent address then; I was still chasing that powder, like a fool, but that was my lifestyle, and I'll

never forget, Miles was in town -- he was working around the corner at a club called [The Crown Phillip.] Billy Joe Powell, and that was the first time I had ever met Powell up close. I had heard about him in Detroit, but he was with Miles -- and Trane was with him, and Philly Red didn't come in town with him for some reason. Billy Joe was with him, and they used Billy Greene, a Chicago pianist, and he worked with them.

Anyway, they told me -- I was away somewhere, I was hanging out on 43rd Street and word got to me that Bobby Paine wanted to see me, so I went out to the Cotton Club, and he said, "Man, this is a telegram and Art Blakey wants you to come to New York." I said, "Oh my God." I didn't want to leave Chicago because I was afraid to go to New York, actually, you know, although I really didn't have nothing in Chicago to hold me there.

So I was talking to Paul about it and he said, "Man, you're going to New York, man -- that's where you need to be." And he hung out with me all that night, and we partied, you know, and what have you -- and took me to the plane the next morning -- a bunch of fellows. I had a shopping bag, a suit somebody give me, a couple of shirts, and that was it.

I threw my outfit away because I contacted him and he said to go to this house when you get in town -- his sister in law's house, and he gives me a pep talk, and he had jobs lined up for me all the way to the West Coast, and we wasn't
gonna -- none of us were gonna use any drugs at all, and blah, blah, blah. Sure.

Anyway, I get to New York and Paul told me in the train station, 'Look, man -- we got a place out in East New York' - they had a little inn out there or something like that -- and he said, 'you can stay out there until you get on your feet', you know; And, because I was trying to find all kinds of excuses not to leave Chicago.

And he said, 'No, man, you need to be in New York.' (Unintelligible). Anyway, I get on the plane to New York, and they had a one nighter down in Washington, D.C. They made it. They had Kenny Drew, Donald Bird, Ira Arnie Sullivan, and I forgot -- he used some bass player down in Washington in my place, but they came back the next morning, and our next engagement would be Washington for a week, and that's where I made it, and still, instead of my buying a suit, he said, 'Well, look, I got a suit', you know; I didn't have a black suit -- and everybody was wearing black suits, and I'm not too tall now, but I'm a little taller than he was, so I had to wear the pants -- the coat wasn't too bad, but the pants was real short on me, you know, and I felt just like sliding off of the bandstand -- when we were finished, oh boy, I acted like I was really in to the music, I didn't pay no attention to that too much, though.
So while we were playing Washington, we got to

Lose Clifford and Richie Powell got killed in an automobile accident. But that was the first engagement That Art Blakey was (inaudible) beautiful, he'd tell Ira and I, "We got to scuffle and we kind of had to scuttle for ourselves now; he said he was gonna put us out on the corner of 52nd and Broadway and said, 'be right back' and then he'd drive off. That's after the engagement.
This was New York?

Well in New York, we knew a lot of musicians, you know, but New York is New York, and he might give you his phone number, but no address. So our money was so tight, we didn't have nothing to get into Even in those big hotels, it wasn't much.
However, I had known some people who knew him, and I went to Brooklyn and I was looking up Willie Jones, a drummer that was working with Mingus, and I had met him out in Chicago.
The same Willie Jones?

The same Willie Jones, that I introduced you to. And, Jackie McLean, Mark Rose, J.R. Monterosa, Mal Waldron, Mel Larkin, and I had met Mingus before so it was just beautiful, because I went to Thelonious' house and he said, "Well, Wilbur, you're in New York now. You thought you was paying some dues in Chicago, but you're gonna pay some dues now in New York." Which I did. But this is my first year time in New York City, and like I said, I settled in Brooklyn, and I went out to a jam session, and

the first two cats I run in to -- jamming with -- was Matthew Bee Gene and Ernie Henry, and Matthew just made a record date for Riverside Records, which was a small company; they had a little storefront office on 49th -- between 9th and 10th or something like that. And, he had only did one side, so he said, 'I want you to make the other side.'

So, I made the other side with him, and that was Grauer and Orrin Keepnews my introduction to Bill, (inaudible). And I met some people from the Music Minus One, another storefront operation, and I made a recording -- Music Minus One. See, but when you made those recordings -- you might make it today, but it might take you anywhere from 2 to 4 weeks to get your money.
Uh huh.
So what are you gonna do in between? You know, the guy could advance you a little something, but it doesn't last any amount of time, especially if you got a Jones, too (inaudible).
No formal contracts?

No. Just a side man.' See, they didn't start getting in to that contract business unless you were a band leader; if you were a band leader and you had copyrighted tunes, then you'd sign a contract. But even as a bandleader, you were just lucky to work; you know, you made some quick money.
Who else was on that date?

Ernie Henry -- on the side I was on, I think a pianist named Al Knight, and I think he had Arthur Taylor on the drums. On that side, I mean, on that record that Jazz by Gee they called it, I think. And Frank Foster and some others on the other side.

But that was the first thing I did for Riverside. And as I started playing around New York out in Brooklyn ... Kenny Dorham, Ernie Henry, people like that -- word of mouth gets around, you know, and like when you work, everybody starts calling you.

And Philly Billy Joe got me one day and he said, 'man, I got a date with you.' Well, I'm kind of getting ahead of myself. When we played the Washington gig, we come back from New York and our next engagement was Atlantic City; see, in between time, I think we ... that's when I did that date with Lee Morgan. No, no ... not yet. That wouldn't be yet. I was still with Artie.

We played Atlantic City for a week. By that time, Donald Bird quit the band. What happened after we made the Washington engagement, we were supposed to play Newport, and Art come up late, but Donald had his car, and Ira and myself and Kenny Drew was riding with Artie, and he got messed up somehow, and we left late to drive up to Newport, and when we got there, the man was-- all you could hear was Louis Armstrong playing When the Saints Go Marching In ; that was the close of the show, and the man said, 'Well, that's the end of it,' (unintelligible) and Art said, 'Well, we got I'm Art Blakey, and this is the Jazz Messengers, and

hung up on the way, and stuff, and the man said, "I'm sorry, but you can't go in." And that was when Donald Byrd stopped it and u Well, Art, said, "I'm sorry, but I got a family and I got to make the gig."
And so the next engagement, he didn't have a trumpet player, so he got a trumpet player named Danny Moore, a young man out of Savannah, Georgia -- living in New York.

Our next engagement was, let's see ... Atlantic City; our next engagement I think was Trenton. Yeah, it was Trenton, New Jersey, and then we had another engagement in Philadelphia. Now, I didn't want to go to Philly, because I had heard that the police were so tough on the addicts or people they thought were addicts, and if you had scars on your arm, you'd go to the penitentiary.
Those were the days of Ferguson.

Yeah. Well, anyway, Kenny Drew and I both said, 'Well, man, you got to get somebody else to make that gig.' And he fumed and screamed and said, 'No, you're gonna make it -- I brought you out of Chicago.' So we finally said, 'Okay'. So we come down to Philly and this was when I was introduced to Lee Morgan. Lee made the gig. Back then, he and Lee were very good buddies, and he played at the old Blue Note.
Now we went up ... the thing was on a Wednesday. Now, I had a hole in my tooth that I was walking around with

this little medication with cotton; that you'd stick down and kill that nerve ... for years. I was deathly afraid of dentists. And Friday night, I'll never forget, I started dancing, this tooth went up on me and started aching, and I couldn't play; I was a nervous wreck, and so Spanky played a night, and some night, Art would pay me off and he would say 'Well man, you didn't want to come down here with me' and blah, blah, blah, and I'm gonna change it.

And he said 'What do you want to do? Go back to Chicago?' And I said, 'No, I'm going back to New York'. So I got used to New York, and that was where I went. I went back to New York and I moved out there with somebody out there in Brooklyn, and that was my initiation. Ira I stayed out for awhile in New York and he was married and had three children, and my kids were kind of grown, so we didn't have no hassle that way, and then I was still chasing that powder (inaudible) and trying to work.
You never recorded with the Jazz Messengers, though?

Oh yes, we did. We recorded once. When we first got to New York. Columbia - Art was signed with Columbia then, and they had some young lady, she was Dutch; she was a vocalist, and I don't know know, Jutta Hipp or what her name was, but I never heard that album. But we made it and we got paid for it. So I don't know ... I never heard it. Donald Byrd, Ira Sullivan, Kenny Drew, myself, and Art Blakey.
Gee, I hope the tape is still around.

Well, they might have it on the shelf somewhere, or it might have been produced in Europe. You know, so who knows? It might come out one of these days, but I remember, that was the only time we recorded.
So you left got the Messengers at that point and went back to New York ...

Yeah, went back to New York, and let me see, I started working a gig around Brooklyn, and little neighborhood bars and what not, and my reputation was being built up, cats were seeking me out, you know, for jobs, and so I went over to Riverside and they were in the process of moving from the storefront to kind of like a garage like structure on 51st -- West 51st, and I asked -- he said something like, I said, 'You're always wanting me to record, so why don't you give me a little job sleeving records' -- you know, putting the records in to the covers; that way I figure I could earn me enough money to keep me in, a place to stay and what not.
So he said, 'Okay' -- so that was my job. And I didn't realize that they wanted to keep (inaudible) -- also, it was like the rhythm section ...
You and Philly Billy Joe.
Philly Billy Joe and Kenny Drew was the rhythm section; we didn't know it at that moment, because

they had -- let's see who else came in? Drew, myself, Philly filled in most of the time; yeah, A.T. a couple of times. But we did an album with Ernie Louie Henry called 'Presenting Ernie Louie Henry' -- Arthur Taylor, Kenny Dorham, [Jim Knight], or whatever. But we made that, and oh, started recording with Dick Stig Johnson, this altoist, Dave McKenna, a pianist, and Billy Joe, and who else? Oh, my goodness, I started recording with everybody they would bring in there.

I'd be downstairs, in the garage, you know, sleeping and he'd say, 'Keepnews All right Wilbur, you got a record date tomorrow -- where's your fiddle?' Now, as long as I'm working, my fiddle was around, you know, but when the office pawn it and is closed, like on a - say, if I'm not working, I'd get it out Monday morning, you know, and that was the fiddle that Oscar Pettiford gave me now, when he saw me in New York.
Because Art took me down to the music store to buy me one.
You mean he had those intentions?

Sure. Pettiford offered he bought this fiddle for me, you know, a beautiful instrument.

He's cutting th e holes. But music is beautiful. It always will be, you know.

I was always partial to the blues (acoustic) ... but nowadays everything is so technical; you know, it seems like they don't want you to look at each other when you're playing, usually, unless you're up on a big concert stage, you know, when you're 25 feet away from each other, there is no closeness there.

Well, I said we did this Chicago Sound, and the next thing I knew they had a big Chicago Sound night down at Birdland. And Wilbur Campbell went back to Chicago, and Frankie Dunlap made one side of the record, too, because Wilbur had to leave the next month after the initial side, and Junior Mance had left, and so we used Kenny Drew down at Birdland, but it was a beautiful night, and amost every other night, I had ... And he called me up for a gig -- Mr. Stan Getz, and Elvin Jones, Wynton Elmer, Joe Kelly and myself, and we were working -- that's Red Garland, Philly Joe, Trane, Paul, and himself opposite the Miles Davis Quintet -- at Birdland.

Naturally, we were gonna cook -- we were gonna play our best, too, and not realizing, you know, Stan Getz -- he's a star; naturally he's a star, but we want to get behind and push him just as much; the rhythm section was pushing Miles. And Stan said, "Nothing" and then looked over at me and say, "Oh, Wilbur? I want to try another bass player." And I said, "Well what for?" and he said, "Well, I do, man?" Now he say he was trying out another bass player each night, he was trying out different bass players, and it wasn't the bass player's fault; it was just that they were playing all that one and three different rhythms and he didn't know where it was at, and as I say, Stan was going through problems, personal problems, and ...

And this particular night, the place was just jammed because you know, I told you, I played drums occasionally, and we were playing and I'm standing right behind Buddy, and when we finished, [unintelligible] I took the subway over and Buddy got up from his set and was bounding toward me with his sticks in his hand, you know, and somebody in the crowd hollered, "Play some drums, Wilbur" and I thought Buddy was offering me the sticks, so I got the sticks out of his hand, and slid in the seat and looked over to the other and said, "I'm taking 8 bars" and I went in to the eight bar solo and I was gonna play some drums. And I was ... like I say, I was kind of established now, recording with everybody during this period, and one day Philly Joe Billy Joe grabbed me one day and said, "Man, come over here to the Blue Note, and make this date with Lee Morlin and Horace Silver and Billy and myself -- it was Lee's first date day, I believe, doin' it, and we did -- called Lee Morlin, and I was fearful because I'm thinking of all this music that Lee got -- and he said, "Man, there ain't nothing to that," and I said, "Yeah, man, come on," and he showed me the parts, passages, and I went in to it, and what not, because I didn't read the notations and such; I could read the chord changes, though.

But they were teaching me like I never studied. But we got through that beautifully, and Alfred Lyon was very enthused -- he started calling me on quite a few record dates, and I got some calls from Herbie Irving Mann and a whole lot of people, different ones, but they had to get permission from in order to use me, and they signed me up with some options. Oh, but that was part of that New York scene.

Things kind of slowed up, and I worked a couple of gigs down at the Fire Spot Fireside and Dave Amram Amarand had a weekend down there with me, and I was in the rhythm section, and it was just a little hamburger joint on the Bowery there; we were

trying to make a little club out of it, and the next weekend, Ray Bryant came in on piano, and the following weekend, Herbie Nichols -- I was able to play with him; he was a genius. Beautiful young man -- not too long before he died. And then Thelonious said, "Come on down," and we with Trane and Shadow went down there, and we played -- and that was the gig. I stayed with that gig, plus recordings, first record it, still at Riverside now, and one night we had a recording date with Gerry Mulligan and Monk, called Mulligan Meets Monk. And we got through with the date and I rushed down to the club from and the recording date, and I hadn't eaten, so I put my fiddle on the bandstand, and I said I was going to go around the corner to get a sandwich; I'll be right back." Trane was there. In Trane

So I went around to this little place and got me a -- I'll never forget -- I should have gotten a hot sandwich, but I got a tunafish salad, ate it, and oh boy, it ate the pit of my stomach and I was sick; so sick I was afraid and I just took a taxi. I made a call ... I called up one of the bass players that lived right around the corner from me, and asked him if he would work in my place, and I went on home. Keepnews

And the next day, Keith says, "What you do?" and Joe Termini told Monk to told me that they were gonna get rid of me; I was unreliable that followed me, but I still made it. They always feel that you couldn't depend (unintelligible) always down on Wilbur Ware, and yet, I would be the first on on the gig.
Strange.
It was strange, I'd be the first one there, on time, ready to play, but they just knew that I was gonna mess up.

Well maybe, the one or two occasions when something did happen, brought that attitude on, like the record with Art Blakey, where Spanky played, in Harlem on My Mind the one ... there's a picture of it -- the one with Sam Dockery.

Yeah, that was on Atlantic. Johnny Griffin joined the Messengers, and it was Art Blakey and the Messengers, with Thelonious. The period after you had gotten sick and the band broke up, you went back with Miles -- and then what did you do?

Well, I started working in gigs of my own -- maybe that was about '57 or '58, and all of '58 I was recording with different people; Clifford Jordan, John Jenkins Jacob, Hank Mobley -- did a whole lot of dates with him --

I was working out in Brooklyn with my own group, and I walked up on the gig, playing drums - Brooklyn - but before then I was working out of the Continental at a club with my own group; the picture on the back of the Chicago Sound, that was taken in that club by a fellow called [Selly] Copeland, he was a male nurse who just happened to take that photo And I think he sold it to Keepnews to put on the album. Were you doing much traveling?
No.
Out of New York?
No, no. During this period, I wasn't traveling nowhere, you know. Nowhere at all. I stayed right there in New York City - just did record dates and club dates, you know, and that was it.
And you stayed there ... this was '59, '60 and on up through that period into the sixties?
No. The latter part of '59, around November, some guy come out of Chicago -- he's dead now --

you know, a fellow named Don[Defore]-- he come up with the big idea that he'd come to New York -- and he had signed Johnny Griffin and Johnny was back in Chicago then, and he wanted Sonny Rollins, and he's gonna get John Coltrane; each one of wanted them to come and play a concert at the University of Chicago. He was promoting it like that.

So he comes and finds me and says, well, you know how people are -- this particular night, I just happened to hanging out in front of the Birdland, and Tommy Potter was working downstairs with somebody, and like, musicians -- we didn't have dressing rooms. I mean in all those big clubs, you didn't have no place where the musicians could go and sit after you got off the bandstand. You couldn't sit at the tables, as that was for customers. And at the back of the service bar, you had to move out the way because the waiters were coming in and taking orders, and you didn't want to stand by the bar all the time, so you'd come outside; you'd come out on the stage.
You'd be ...

That's right. You come out, you know, and that meant the guys would go in some other bar or restaurant or somewhere and watch the clock in order to get back for your next set. So I came upstairs with Tommy Potter and here's this wild looking dude running up and he says, 'Say Tom, do you know where I can find Wilbur Ware?'

He said, 'Man, I got a job for him out of Chicago, and I can't find him.' So Tom looks at me and I look at Tommy, and Tommy said to him 'You know Wilbur Ware?' -- and he says, 'Yeah, man, I'm from Chicago; I know Wilbur. Do you know where I can find him?'

And Tom says, 'But you do know Wilbur, don't you?' and he said, 'Yes, I know him'; and he said, 'Well, what you want with him, man?' and he showed me this placard that he's got with my name all over it and Johnny Griffin and Jody Christian and Phil Thomas on drums, and the next one was gonna be Sonny Rollins with the same rhythm section, and he said, 'Man, if you know where he's at, please tell him' and I said, 'Well, man I am Wilbur Ware.' But all I could do was just laugh, and Tommy said, 'Yeah?' and 'You knew him, huh?' And he said, 'Well, man ... you know how it is.' -- and do you know that I stayed with that cat; that cat would not let me out of his sight. And, you know, that he went down to the Western Union, and he sent off for the money to get the tickets, and he said, 'You're not getting out of my sight; you going back to Chicago.' Just like that.
Maybe you could talk; before you get in to that too much, maybe you can talk about this Sonny Rollins date that was at the Vanguard; that's an important date.
Oh yes. The night at the Village Vanguard.
Yeah.

Oh, well, one afternoon; no, the previous afternoon, I'm down at the Vanguard and Sonny had come up and he we had a bass player, Don Bailey, out of Baltimore, and La Roca Pete the drummer; they were working with Sonny, and Sonny said, "Hey Wilbur, I want you to come by tomorrow afternoon" -- now they had matinees down at the Vanguard at that time, and he said he was recording down there tomorrow and I want you to come by and do a track on my date."

And he said, "But I'll pay you for the whole date". It wasn't that much -- you know, a whole day I think. It was $50 or $75 or something like that. One side. And two sides, LP was a hundred and a quarter, I believe.

But anyway, I said, "Okay" and he said, "And you don't have to bring your bass" he said to Don, and Don said "Will it be all if he uses yours?" right for you here?" he and I said, "Yeah, that'd be fine."

So the next afternoon, I show up. Elvin Evelyn is sitting there, and so we're sitting there at the table, and Rudy Van Gelder's I look up there and they got all this equipment set up in Alfred Lion and Don and Pete are waiting on line, and Sonny. No, down in peak with Sonny and Sonny comes in and he doesn't say a word to us, he just walks back and goes on up toward the stage, so I'm thinking, I think, well, he's going up there and he'll want me to play a set, a warmup, and then call us to play whatever go into the tune he wants played.
So Pete sits down at the drums, and Don grabs his bass, and this is a live recording, and Sonny walks out to the

microphone. center stage, and says, "Will Elvin Evan Jones and Wilbur Ware come to the bandstand please?" and it was just like that. So, you know. Pete and Donald had to get up and they came back looking at us, odds but they knew we were gonna play, so it was just the idea that we would play first, so we get up there and Sonny turned to me and says, "I want to play Old Devil Moon" I said, "Wait a minute, Sonny; I'm not too sure of the changes on that one." and (unintelligible) and he laid some changes on me. I hadn't played the tune; I had heard it, but I hadn't played it to remember it well enough to record it, and he said, "Oh, you can hear it."

So I said, "Okay, let's take it" -- and we went from that in to something else; played the whole thing, the whole first side, and then he says, "Look," while they was changing the tapes, "I had to call these fellows up, you know, they were working with me and I want to let them play a tune", and I said, "Isn't that something?" He hired Elvin Evan and I just to play one track and here we wound up playing the whole gig date except for one track '.

But, you know, Elvin Evan and I thought, you know, since it wasn't rehearsed no emergency; it was spontaneous, a good feeling, thing, "Oh, this ain't nothing," but Sonny seemed to sense something; he felt real comfortable with what he was doing, because he asked us; he said, "Look man, I'm going on tour and I'm going out to the West Coast and from there I'm going to Paris, and I want you all to stay with me; I'll take care of

this, and anything you need, I'll get for you'. And I said, "No, man, I don't want to go." And that would have been my first chance to go to Europe. But heck, I was recording, you know, at Riverside and I didn't want to leave.
And when I made that album, they still say everybody heard thinks of that as a kind of a classic.

Well, he has said that that was an historic album in the sense that I guess, without the piano being able to do the things and that he could do, he said he could do it with a good bass player, and that is important. And then as we reach the other ... More from at the Vanguard, that was recorded at that same time.

That was recorded that night. The first group of tunes was in the afternoon, and that More from the Vanguard was later on that night, when everybody was retiring, and you know, and I guess he had to pick whether he wanted to put out, you know, the editing, and he just put these out, and it was a year ago? Or something like that ... a couple years ago.

But still some people like it. That's what is happening now. A whole lot of these recording companies they have, the thing where they make one master, two masters, and they put them out, you know; you approve one master and that's it. So of late, they been bringing out two or three different takes of the same tune.
And the recording company is making all the money.

Well, they didn't always make the money, you know, unless you had a business agent or an accountant, that was .. the little groups they didn't have no business sense on them; they didn't know how to protect their rights or whatever, you know, and you had a chance to be heard, you know, and you just did it; it was work.

That's just like the guys, you catch the kids now, they figure that all they have to do to be stars is get on a record, make a record, I want to make a record, and that's it.
But that's true now.

Yeah, but it isn't always that way. You can make a record, and unless you plan it, and you know, have the right engineers and all this right ingredients, it ain't going nowhere, unless one of those big companies really want to push you, and they don't care how good the record is.

My friend Clifford Jordan got an album that I'm really crazy about, and that's called 'Starting Time' -- it's out of one of those pseudo-companies out of Riverside, Jazzland, and that was recorded in '61, and just because every tune on there just about belongs to Clifford, they haven't reissued it, and to me, that's one of the cleanest sounds songs; one of the swingiest albums I've done -- and very happy to have been on that date. That was the date with Cedar Walton, Kenny Dorham, Tootie Heath, Kenny Walden, Tudy Heath ...

But, even though they haven't re-issued it, we saw it a couple years ago in a record store on the lower East Side for twenty-some dollars, and it's not as old as some of the older ones that were reissued.

Yeah. Well, like Riverside of Japan is bringing out a whole lot of old Riverside records, you know, and well, it's big business. The conglomerates are doing it. I was reading this periodical call Black Perspectives and this guy, Frank Kofsky wrote ....
The Black Perspective in Music?

Yeah. He wrote an article in there called "The State of Jazz" and he is very informative about who owns what, and which way jazz, as I know it, is headed, came to be, and he is not a musician, but he can take time to check all those facts where, as a musician, it's hard for us to get to the material, you might say.

But we know what's going on, just like I was saying being a musician and coming off the bandstand, the club owner looked like he wanted to hide you somewhere -- when you're not in the club, go anywhere, just get out of my sight, you know.

But this is something that should have been dealt with by some other people, perhaps, and you can't expect a musician to create the music, to take care of the business, and do all that, even though people somehow expect that, I think it's too much to expect.
It is. Now you can't create nothing worrying about how many people come in the club and things like that.
Well, even like Duke Ellington, with his -- he had a fantastic business sense along with his music, but even he had to have other people to help him. He just couldn't do everything else himself.

You can't, right. You go pick up the guys and ... I know bandleaders who tried to, you know, some cats they couldn't depend on, but they needed them because they could play. They would pick them up and do things like that just to make sure he would get to the gig on time. Even Leo. You know, Leo had a suit that I could wear it, as well as Nicky Hill Gilbert could. We didn't have a decent suit to look right on the bandstand, but Leo had his suit pressed, and I'd say there it is, and he made sure there were some holes in it so we couldn't pawn it. You know.

But that was important, even up until the sixties. In the sixties, people started to, well, I can't really say not caring how they looked -- but they started looking like the general society looked. It wasn't important to dress up anymore in the sixties when you saw them up on the bandstand. In informal attire, but earlier on, you did have to look a certain way.
Well, you had to look like an entertainer;
you would look like an entertainer, because it was a certain amount of flash, you know.

So we arrived and he took me out to his house and he was staying on the South Side, and he said, now you just lay here and we've got to do a couple of promotions and we're going down to see Marty Pay and Daddy O' Dayley down at the studio, and we're gonna publicize these events. And he put signs up

So I'm making contact with all those folks, you know, everybody that hadn't seen me, since I made my big debut in New York; however, I didn't have a fiddle, naturally. I'll buy you one." (inaudible) and at the time, I found out that Malachi who I knew at the time, was working in with we were going at it as a trio, and Andrew Hill, and he had a fiddle that he wanted to sell, so Karl bought that for me, so I had myself another fiddle to play these engagements.

Now, I don't realize that De Fore Duflores (phonetic) was having problems with the black local there; local 208; that was before they merged, and they wanted him to put up so much money and he wouldn't do it. Anyway, we played. It wasn't a good turnout but we got paid; I got paid, you know, Griffin got paid, Phil Thomas got paid and Jody Jerry got paid and, Henry Richard Brown was the walking delegate; walking around with his [twisted] leg, you know, and that knocked the concerts out, because he

Rollins; couldn't contact Sonny Robinson; he was supposed to come in, Coltrane maybe about a week later, or two weeks later, and Cole Train was supposed to come in two or three weeks following that; you know, just as singles, to use our rhythm section. So, that folded.

So I'm stuck in Chicago now, but I'm happy to be home. I got a chance to relax some; I'm staying at his house, and I was kind of babysitting, because they had a little girl there, and when Don and his wife would cut out, I'd sit with the baby and have a few friends over, you know, and that was it. And I wanted to get around and see somebody, and started visiting some of the old guys in the neighborhood; went over to see there was a club called McKee's Chris Anderson and Leo, and (unintelligible) and they'd bring Sutherland in different bands, and as well, the Southern Hotel. Sixties?

Then all of a sudden, that riot started. And oh boy, that broke up the Newport thing. But we come back to New York, and they got a theatre over on the east side, that the Jazz Artists give, and we were gonna play jazz concerts nightly, you know, but we couldn't get no publicity, nobody to handle us, you know? come out and nobody would touch us. So the act folded.

And I started going around to different clubs; I went around to the Five Spot Firespot, and (unintelligible) and Jim Harlo, Hall, and who was there but Jimmy Giuffre, Jim and who was it that was on drums ... oh, the drummer, and Buell Neidlinger, Bill Nyad, a bassist that I knew; a white dude, that had been working mostly with Cecil Skeets Taylor. And we were buddies. But I went in and I sat in with Giuffre for Dupree, and Giuffre Dupree wanted me to open up with him down at the Vanguard, and I didn't tell you this story, but back in the late fifties, '59, I hung strung out there in Harlem, and I come over to Brooklyn, and I had all my clothes and what not in this pawn shop, and I was going over there to get -- the guy knew me and all, I needed a few dollars, and I said, "Come on man, add some more on to the ticket, you know, and I'll come and get my stuff, you know," and he said, "No, I can't do that." Anyway, I wound up bad-off mad, and my sickness was coming down on me again, so I was walking passed this club, in the Club Baby Grand Brooklyn, and a guy with a fiddle was standing up on stage, and I just walked in there and took it out, took it down to the next block, and walked in there and took out my identification and pawned it for $50. And I said whoever's fiddle this is, they would know that I got it, and they know that I didn't try to sell it or nothing, so not to worry about it, you know. I had pawned it before, and once I pawn it, the word would

But however, naturally, we had to report it to the police, and that's when they started looking for me. That was before I went to Chicago, and I'm not thinking about that so much, because I knew he got his fiddle the next day; he got it back, but the police was still looking for me for petit petty larceny. And it didn't come to the floor until I got back there in '60, and I played the Newport thing, and I was getting ready to join Jimmy Giuffre Jitfree (phonetic) and that's when the cabaret licenses were enforced then, and you had to have that cabaret license in order to work a nightclub.

And, at that particular time, Frank Sinatra, as well as Sophie Tucker refused to work in New York in those big rooms unless they abolished that cabaret card business. And that made the police department mad, and they started going around raiding the clubs, and whoever had any kind of minor bust, you know, they were snatching their cards from them.

So naturally we had to look out for everything, so "I'll meet you in the morning, Jimmy says to me, we're gonna go down in the morning to get your cabaret card straightened out, you know, and reissue it to you because it had elapsed, and he said, "Yeah man, I got a Buell fiddle that you can have" -- and give me a bass. And he ended Allen Eager had given up getting me an apartment, and I was living there right on

West Broadway, and next morning, Jimmy comes by dutifully, and we go down to the license bureau, and sitting up there, the man says, "Oh yeah, Wilbur Ware -- have a seat." He says to me, "We'll get your card straightened out for you in a few minutes." So I'm sitting and sitting, and Jimmy said, "Well, what's the trouble?" and he says, "Oh, we're getting to it" and pretty soon here come two detectives. They called out to Brooklyn. And the come in and said, "Oh, here's that bass fiddle snatcher we been looking for." All because of Sinatra, or anything they can do to harass, you know, so naturally I didn't get the job; they carted me out to the jail out there in Brooklyn.

And they were really picking on us, and Peck said, "Man, I don't want to see the man in jail, and he said, 'I've seen Wilbur, and I did see him out in Chicago -- he came out there to play a concert.' One of those jazz festivals, you know? And he asked me when I was gonna pay him his money and I said as soon as I start making some money, and he said, okay. Well, I squared it with him ... but the police wanted to make a big thing out of it, and he said 'I don't want to prosecute him', and he told them, "He's gonna pay me back'.
But the police said to him, "Oh, we can't do that; we did a whole lot of work on this case' -- a whole lot of BS!
Right.
And so I had laid up there in that jail

for almost 90 days. It's time I go to court, and he's telling the judge that he didn't want to prosecute me or nothing, and the judge said, 'No, he's got to plead guilty to something.' In other words, I had to cop out. So finally I said okay. He says, 'Well, you have 5 more days here.' 'How long you been in already?' and I say, '85 days', and he says, 'Well, you got to do 90 days, and that 5 more days must be served', and so I had to lay in jail for five more days!

When I come out, just before that, a great big snowstorm hit New York, and I'm out there in a summer suit; this was about in '61, and anyway, A Jones A was working over there at a hotel with somebody, and anyway, I come out and a friend of mine, Billy Howell, a trombone player, living on the upper West Side, he got me a room over there, and that's when they had what they call 'drug panic' -- couldn't find no drugs nowhere.

But that was good because I had a chance to clean up; my body got clean, and that's when I was doing a whole lot of recording for the Blue Note during that period, too. A I had done many things with Grant Greene, and I did some with Hank during that period, and I got myself together, and did I go out to Chicago again? This was about '61. In the summer, anyway, I did the thing with Clifford Jordan, started an album, and a few other things.
So I went on up there and my health started failing;

this was about in '62; I was gigging, around, you know, just little gigs here and there. In 1963 I got so I couldn't go up stairs; I'd get out of breath, you know, I was coming down with TB. You know, I always believed that you had TB, you'd be spitting up blood, but it hadn't reached that stage, and (unintelligible) a lady friend of mine saw me during this time, "You don't look good; and said, 'come on, let me take you to Bellevue', and I said "Oh, I will go tomorrow", and she said, "No, I will go with you right now." I went over there and the man said, "Oh!" and they rushed me upstairs. So she left me in Bellevue, and I stayed there, oh, a couple weeks. And then I was in there awhile, and he said, "You better?" and I say, "Yeah" and he said if I really didn't feel better to tell the contact man and they would send me upstate, you know, and get better treatment and be able to get an allotment check, or something like that.

So I said sure, and when the contact man got through, I told him I remember my army serial number, naturally, and a couple of weeks later, they sent me up to Castle Point, New York -- up around Newburgh... somewhere up in there. The Veterans Hospital. And when I got up there, oh, I was doing good; again, I had a chance to start eating right and getting my rest, and my TB was at the point where they caught it in time

where they didn't have to do any major operations, you know, they said I had a whole lot of little holes in my lung, and with rest, in about a year's time I would be all right. And oh, it was nice ... the fresh air I appreciated it, and I had time to think; I had records that I would play, and of course, I was in close touch with my family; my mother, and she was about to have an operation for gall stones. Now I had been in the hospital then 8 months.

So about in the middle of the night, about 12 o'clock one night, my brother calls me crying, saying, "Mama's gonna go in the hospital tomorrow!" and I said, "Oh, you fool -- you didn't even know your mother was as ill as she is."

So I told the doctor I wanted to be of some help to my mother, you know, so I signed out and finished my little stay out there in a hospital in Chicago. He said okay, and I did. I went home, and my mama came home from the hospital all right, and I had gone out to Hines and stayed out there until they discharged me. And they put me on some medication, which I stayed on for quite a few years.
Now this was in '63 and '64, I was there ... I was discharged from the Veterans Hospital. So, I'm back in Chicago in '64-'65 and in '66 Mama died then, and I had no other
place to go. By then I was not even thinking about using no drugs; all I'm thinking about is drinking. I really learned how to drink when I was in that Veterans Hospital. You know how the guys do.

However, I went from one extreme to another, and I came back to New York in August of 1967, and while I was in Chicago -- now this was around '65, a young man I met up in New York in my dope fiend days, said I did him a favor one day. He was ill, and he spoke to me, and I had just copped, and said would I turn him on, and I said sure, come on. And I saw him in Chicago and he told me, he said, "You don't remember me, but you helped me one time" and he asked me where I was going and I told him, "Man, you ain't supposed to be in this kind of shape, so look, give me your phone number and I'll call you in a couple days."

So I give him Mama's phone number, and about a week later I'm over at the house and the phone rings and it's this cat Tommy, and he says, "Wilbur, I'm coming over. I'm gonna buy you a bass." And I said, "Oh, man ..." and he said, "No, I'm serious" and he said, "Get your coat ready" and we came on down. This was in November 1965, I believe. So we came down; he was on the South Side and he had to come up to 1898 Milwaukee Avenue -- that was my mother's apartment over there, and I get in the car and he says, "Where's the best place?" and I knew of a bass shop called Kagen and Kane, and I said, "Now man, wait

a minute, what you want from me? I said, 'You're not A.. I said, a horn or something like that.' What you want me to do; get a group together for you to manage it?' He said, 'No man, I just want you to have a weapon.' And to me, that was a beautiful statement; he said, 'You're a bass player and you should be out here playing, you know, and you're running around drinking this wine like you're crazy,' and he said, 'Come on.'

So we get down there and he says to pick one out, German and Czech so I'm checking out the basses, and I said to the salesman, 'How much do you want for that,' and he says $350 ... no, he says $450, and he says, 'Well, look, I'll give you $350 cash, and I say, 'Hold it, hold it,' you know, I say, 'This guy is nice enough to buy this and I know that we can go to the pawn shop and it wouldn't cost more than a hundred and some dollars.'

So I told him that and he said okay, you win. So I say, yeah, and we get in the car and we go out there to 47th and Prairie to Willis to a pawn shop Pond Shop, an outlet and they had a fiddle in there in an old [unintelligible] blonde case, and it didn't have no strings on it, naturally, and no cover, and I asked him how much he wanted for it, and he said, 'Oh, give me a hundred twenty-five' and Tommy said okay, and we went back downtown and got some strings, got a beautiful cover and a pick and the man fixed it up for me, and he said, 'Now let's go' -- and asked me about my union card, and I told him, and he went and shelled out $85 for that local 208.
Local 208?

Yeah ... to straighten me out, you know. Then he took me over to the side and he says you shouldn't be staying there; you should have a place here on the south side, so the cats can get to you more readily and you'd be able to go out and play more, you know.

And he did all that just because I helped him once, and actually, that's what some of the musicians are about. At one time, they used to help each other, you know? And the same way when you was uptight, and you'd go down to his job on his pay nights, and he'd help you.
Of course it doesn't happen like that no more; when these guys see you now they sneak off, you know.
Like the thing that was in the paper recently where the guys were awarded money for not getting paid at all ... like Marvin Gaye.
