But I said, "Okay, I'll go." He didn't really have to twist my arm too much. I wanted to see what Newport was like. I hadn't been up there since the riot. Anyway, we took off that night. We got to Newport the next afternoon and they had us sandwiched in. He had Howard Johnson on tuba. He had Grachan Moncur on trombone, himself on tenor, and he had a poet, crazy guy, Leon Bibbs (PHONETIC) -- not Leon Bibbs, but --
Leroy.
Leroy Bibbs. He's nuts. He was in the same vein, you might say, Lenny Bruce and all the cats like that, which you would call -- I won't say beat poet, a hippie
poet, a revolutionary poet, whatever.
Right.

Anyway, they had sandwiched us in between -- they was waiting on Clark Terry's big band to show up and Elvin and Jimmy Garrison and Joe Farrell was playing before we was scheduled to come on and, oh, they did it. Elvin sounded so beautiful. Standing ovation and we had to follow them. I didn't even take a bass up there because I figured I could borrow somebody's bass. I was asking Joe Benjamin (PHONETIC) -- Joe Benjamin was going to play next with Clark Terry, so I asked him can I use his bass. He said, 'No, you should have brought yours.' Jimmy Garrison said, 'Man, here, take my fiddle,' which was beautiful. Jimmy was like that. And we played and George Weim Williams (PHONETIC) only let us play one tune, but we played that and played it well. Had a conga player Muhammed Ali, who happened to be Rashid Ali's brother.

From that moment on, every job that Archie Shepp would get, he'd call me. 'Mr. Ware --' record dates, jobs, we played up in Buffalo. They had some whole week of music, quite a few groups -- Cannonball, Mongo, Tito Puente (PHONETIC). Philly Billy Joe Jones worked with us, Archie Shep (PHONETIC), Tommy Turrentine and little blind Chris Anderson and Joe Lee Wilson. That's the group that Archie Shepp took up.
No rehearsal. We just went up there and played. But it was good gigs, you know? That was around '68. All the

while, Clifford Jordan is hooking up a tour of Europe he wants me to go on. He called me from Europe. He left and went over there. He called me, "Many they wanted a brochure on you and he got a string of gigs over here. Told me the price and all that. I wasn't ready for it, so I wouldn't go. I'm still working in New York around this time. Eddie Blackwell came by my house. He stayed right around the corner from me. He said, "Man, Monk wants you to work with us." So, that was a joy, to work with the T again, openly at the Vanguard. So we made that Vanguard gig, Archie Shep -- not Archie, but Archie Shep must be talking about me.

Monk, Blackwell, Charlie Rouse (PHONETIC) and I think that was the last time Charlie worked with T. Thelonius was kind of ill and he was saying things that really hurt Charles' feelings, but we made the weekend -- no, we made that week and then Monk went into the hospital. This was all '68 mostly. And I'm working down at Slugs with different little groups and I worked with Sonny Rollins down at the Vanguard. Al Foster, Al Daley (PHONETIC), myself.

I know one night Tony Williams was in the house. Miles was in the house, too, you know. He was kind of in his bag. He was, you know, just standing around. He was speaking and whatnot. Sonny was staring standing off into space and Al Foster and I come out -- we had a beautiful set -- come off the stand, come back in the kitchen. Tony Turner say, "You guys are cats
going to get fired." I say, "For what, man?" He say, "You're playing too much."
(Laughter.)

And sure enough, we didn't have a gig the next week. But that was all right. Sonny had a thing. He had a thing, he told me, the last time I played with him, we went to play a benefit over in Newark. This was about '72. He say, "Wilbur, you ain't going to start on me tonight." I never looked at it that way. I figured that whenever you get up on the bandstand, you do your best and you put your best foot forward and it wasn't that I would try to outplay anybody. If I'm happy, he's inspiring me and I'm going to inspire him. Piano players, the drummer, whatever, I'm going to play my best, regardless. That's the way I feel. It's the only way I could play.
It's funny. If the band around me, if they not playing, I can't play.

Right. Well, with Sonny Rollins Robbins, at that time, perhaps it was his nervousness, too, but you have to remember what you accomplished musically, which people constantly are saying. Like David Baker talks about he teaches people what you have contributed to the music. Maybe we could talk about different styles of bass playing and different peoples' contributions, because it's not clear to the average person.
Oh, yeah, well, like I said, I came out of the mold of Blanton and Israel Crosby (PROPHETIC) and a few

others -- Truck Chuck Parham (PHONETIC), John Kirby Curved (PHONETIC), oh, even Milt Hinton. Well, they all give me something, you know, with which to grow. I noticed the younger bassists, you hardly hear them mention the great bassists like Paul Chambers, you know, or Ray Brown, for that matter. Most of the young bassists don't say nothing. They hardly say anything about Oscar Pettiford. But most all the youngsters, I can tell that they followed Paul. Paul was the master. He was the master with the bow, but it was his concept and he made an extention of the bass with a horn like figures (unintelligible), you know, sound like a horn. That's why you hear the drummer play right along with him. He just keeps swinging.

Well, the way I play bass -- I'm speaking about myself -- I'm more percussive. I'd rather the drummer lay out, so I can create something. I know where I'm at mostly at all times, you know, and it's up to the guys around me to know where they at, musically. If they're going to -- if we're playing together and I take a solo and I have them all laying out, they should follow me, you know, know where I'm at. I might play two choruses, but I'm playing two choruses, you know? Whatever.
Anyway, talking about Paul, master musician, beautiful bassist and I've seen so many cats come out of his mold. Mingus was mean. He's a mean bassist, you know.
Well, his strength seems to be more in his
arrangements than it is his actual fiddle playing.

That's true. Well, he's fast, you know. He used to be fast, whatever you want to call it, fast, but he's creative. I always loved that tune of his called "Mingus Fingers." He did it while he was working with Lionel Hampton. I remember that well. That's when I first met him.
But he has a reputation, too, with the big band. But his eccentric reputation (inaudible) Duke or whatever.

Well, you can say he's a genius. He's kind of eccentric, you know, but deep down, he's a sweetheart. He's a beautiful person. He's been frustrated in a whole lot of ways. So he lashes out the best way he know how, you know? Might be kind of dumb at times, but that's the way he is. He's just being real.
Himself.
Uh-huh.

But people have talked about your playing that played with you. For instance, people like Blumenthal (PHONETIC) that write, writers, but then it's difficult to talk about critics like some people say the only good critics and bad critics -- they're naturally going to reflect their point of view and what they understand about music. But then someone like Billy Howell would come along, who is not a critic, who is an educator and musician himself, and talks
about how you use simple harmonies. Well, he sees it as a harmonic sense. You talked about percussion. But how about that?
Well, --
(Laughter.)

-- it's hard for me to explain because I really don't know, you know. I come up with those little quartets, singing, you know, and I can hear certain things and I try to apply them, you know? For me to even try to say actually what I did musically, it's very difficult. Because I really don't know.
But you can feel it. Like Chris says, he might hear certain thing, you might hear it another way, play it another way.

That's true, that's true. Like it's hard for me to play the same thing twice exactly alike. It's hard to do because I never studied that way. I've never really studied or practiced like you see some people get up and practice, half the day, half the night, and when I practice, I'm practicing while I'm working.
But Richard Davis says that he practices -- or Ron Carter, for instance, says that he practices an awful lot.
Yeah, well, those kind of cats do. I remember Richard in Chicago, way before he left, I first met him. He invited me over to his house and he had the books be-

fore him and he was up in his room, big beautiful collie dog. Richard would get up there and he'd practice six, seven hours. That was the applied -- I guess that's what his teachers told him he'd have to do in order to master his instrument. But see --
How do people reconcile the concept? Because playing -- classically trained bassists and, for lack of a better term -- a jazz bassist, they're two different approaches to the instrument.

Well, that's true. But if you notice now, most of the musicians coming out, they're more technical because they got schools for it. They're learning it, see, and before, when I was coming along, you might drop out of school because you had to earn some money just to live. Now the kids can go, go to high school -- it's there if they want to go. You know, they can -- they got teachers to teach them certain things and if you see someone with some talent, might give him a scholarship, you know? So long as his family's working or earning a living, they can keep going to school. You don't have to drop out to help the family live, you know.

Like I did, I dropped out because I needed clothes to wear, you know? So, I learned a different way. But all the kids coming up now, they know the books. They don't know nothing about the feel, but they know the technique. Then they want to go back to get the feeling. Most of them figure they don't need
the feeling.

But then, too, there's a problem that Chris talks about is there's no guarantee of where they'll go back to. It's like Stanley Clarke (PHONETIC) never having heard of John Kirby. Because the collective improvisation, that approach to playing the fiddle is not taught. There's no guarantee what people will learn or where they'll go.

Well, that's true, but most of them think, "Oh, I know music backwards and forward," you know, that they qualify to play anything. But that's not the way it is really. To play just straight-ahead music. Anybody can write anything for you. They write solos for guys and they can play them. I marvel at the fact that Paul Jeffrey (PHONETIC) give me a record date back there in '72, you know, after you and I met, and Paul did all the arrangements on that. I'm looking at the music; he knew (unintelligible) to write chord changes for me and so he's using Stanley and myself, two basses. I'm listening to Stanley and Stanley say, "You want me to play this?" Stanley just playing it just like you read a book.
Right.

And I mean, it was beautiful. So that's -- and he was only 20, at the most. That's the type of young musicians we're getting now, you know. To me, bass players are ahead in that way. They playing -- what was they playing? Beautiful, you know. They don't have the kind of bottom that
I would like or prefer, but that's me, you know. Technology has got to move on, you know?

But even with technology, blues people are coming back to basics. They're coming back to the bottom in all phases of our existence, not just musically. It seems to me that perhaps even musically, the young people are going to have to go back eventually.
Well --

And learn that. It's like learning to -- it's like going to school and learning how to talk and not learning how to write. Eventually, you're going to have to learn how to write. You have to come back to that if you're going to exist in this society.
Well, it's just like, in order for me to exist in this society, I should learn how to read, you know?
It's mandatory.

Mandatory. If you don't know how to read, you're not really going to make it. It's just like any profession. In order for you to push a proper broom, you've got to have a degree of some sort. It's coming to that.
Well, people that didn't learn that way, like Sam Dockery, Sam said he went back --
Uh-huh.
-- learned how to read, so now he could teach. He has to work. He has to live. There aren't any more
it seems, gigs, scenes- for people that don't know how to read.

Well, I noticed that they're pushing electrical instruments more and more. The average musician has to be an electrical engineer in order to play music. That's what it seems like it's coming to. But progress, go ahead.
Until somebody pulls the plugs.
Yeah, that's what Vernel said.

Well, what about the avant garde. You touched on it a little bit with Archie Shepp and the people like Leroy Jones has written books and you span the entire spectrum in a sense, when they talk about you. For instance, Leroy Jones said you've been around. You're the prime innovator, but you've been around so long, people have had a chance to pick up. So when they talk about you, they talk about really the entire history of black music, black sophisticated music, on the level we're talking about. So how do you feel about avantgarde or making a record with say, with Archie Shepp, or with like (unintelligible) Beautiful Things, which is classified strictly avantgarde.

Well, personally, avantgarde, like they say, is outside, you know. For a while, I believed that they did that to keep what they said cats was stealing their music. It was that black-white thing again. So they said they going to play something that they won't be able to steal, which was a lie, and if you notice now, the avantgarde is actually Euro-
pean. You know, it's what -- it's what it's all about.
(Recording interruption.)

What I mean by it's all about. Back in the '60s, there was these guys. I remember they had a discussion on avantgarde versus jazz. That goes back to what they call Dixieland, with what would you say? Jazz? Dixieland or either swing versus bop, you know.
(Inaudible) all the way back?
It's always a new sound. Jazz and rock.
Well, why is it necessary, do you think, to categorize in that way?

Well, big business, you know. It's just like, you say, this is new, this is something new. When what they say be-bop come out, they was able to sell a whole lot of berets and horn-rimmed glasses. Big business. Economics. Rock, they were able to sell a whole lot of blue jeans.
(Laughter.)
Oh, yeah.
You understand?

But it's as though the thing itself exists and the exploitation of the thing is labeled. You know what I mean? Like the music existed. People used it and start playing it and call it Dixieland, but it already existed before that.
Before the label was tacked onto it.
Before it was accepted.

Or exploited. It's funny when you talk about accepting, which may be part of the problem. Over the years, you see people ask for acceptance, in a sense, like Rahsaan. He was involved in that. People want to get exposed in music and get on television and so forth, but accepting it on different terms, because as far as people, if you look in the Encyclopedia Brittanica or you look up the word jazz, it will say something to the effect that it started in the black experience and it's now American music. That's a point of view. That's an American point of view.
So that when they see Benny Goodman and call him the King --
Of Swing.

King of Swing, they're serious about that. That is their point of view and they'll take somebody like Max Roach (PHONETIC) who say, "Well, hey, I don't see it that way at all." But his is another point of view. It's a black point of view.

Uh-huh. Well, it's going back to that black-white thing again. You notice most of the critics, they'll say, "Which is the better music? A black one or a white one?" You know, that's just like asking which came first, the chicken or the egg, you know.
Naturally white people are going to prefer white people.
(Laughter.)
And black people are going to prefer black people.
That's the whole thing.
But you get somebody like -- what's the drummer's name? Was talking about he was looking for the source? Mel ?.
Yeah, that cat's been around for years.
If people are completely honest, then they recognize the true or the original source.
He went to Africa to find the source and he knows.
But you've worked with everybody -- black, white.

Yes, I have worked with quite a few and I'm thankful that I have. I worked -- I'm going to tell you one gig with Bob Dorough (PHONETIC). He's a pianist, singer, the one that said (unintelligible) he said he did some things with Miles, which he did. Bob Dorough called me up and Al Schachtman, I believe it is -- he was the guitarist with Nina Simone when she first hit the scene. They had a bar mitzvah to play out in -- it wasn't, not Queens -- out in Long Island somewhere. Well, it was right around the corner from Milt Hinton's house, because Milt let me use one of his fiddles to make the gig.
I'm the only brother there and so when Al and Bob

start playing all these Jewish tunes, there wasn't no -- how did I know how to play it, you know? It just comes naturally to me because when I come up, like I said, hustling us-men around Chicago, we had to play everything. We go in clubs and somebody ask us, you know, for tunes. We've heard them. Somebody would sing them to us. We'd learn it right there, you know? That stuck back in my memory bank, you might say. Just like Clifford Jordan and I had a job one St. Patrick's night, up in the 90s. They had Tootie Heath on drums, Marvin Stamm on trumpet, Clifford on tenor and myself on bass, no piano, because it was just a regular Irish bar, up there on 1st Avenue up in the 90s.
Good gig. A lady come up to us. Would you play, 'When Irish Eyes Are Smiling?' Clifford turned to me and said, "Now, how did that go?"
(Laughter.)

So, I started singing it and playing. You know, I didn't play the melody. I didn't have no bow to try to bow the melody, but I started singing it and playing accompaniment. It's just a waltz, you know, that Clifford got the idea what was happening. Marvin knew it, but he was being cool.
(Laughter.)
You couldn't play -- you know, it was just a neighborhood gig, you know, but they wanted all Irish tunes.
Right.

And I'm happy to be able to do things like that. Sometimes you can make or break a band and have somebody in that band that knows some of those tunes that somebody might want. We had a little gig back in the '40s, when I come out of service, a cat named Mike Walker, saxophone was his instrumentation -- saxophone, guitar and bass -- we worked up on this job about six months. Every night, at least twice a week, this guy would come in and as soon as he walked in the door, he wanted to hear Milenbergy Milenburg Joys. I don't care what we were playing, when we'd see him approach that door to come in, we'd go right into Milenbergy Milenburg Joys. That was a $10 tip each time. So to be able to play those kind of tunes.
Then it got to the point where some of the so-called hip cats won't play the requests, you know. They didn't want to admit they didn't know them.
Right.
That would alienate some of the audiences. But that's all part of that avantgarde versus swing, be-bop, whatever.

You're kind of used to seeing that in the neighborhood, moreso, it seemed, where you'd go in and you may get a star working with some local guys and they may not be able to play [it's author?] music. But this is more far-reaching than that, because these are people that are on the national scene, so to speak.
The avantgarde people, you speaking of?
Yes, indeed.

Well, yes, they up there. But that's what they -- they supposed to be -- avantgarde, the average public ain't supposed to understand nothing they're playing. It's a so way out. Most of the public don't understand, but they're going along with the images. "Yes, I know exactly what's happening." And the guy's standing up there, just take a deep breath and blow a whole lot of notes, and that's it.
How much do you think Trane contributed to that, because you were talking about the latter '60s and when cities were --
In turmoil.

-- in turmoil and the revolutionaries were talking about John Coltrane, his book of poetry. If you collected all the things that were written in the '60s on Trane, you could have a nice anthology just on him from the poetry.

Well, Trane was searching for something. Trane -- musically, Trane played everything. He had played it all, played with everybody. So he was searching for another sound, another way of getting over his horn, you know? At times, he was booed by people that, you know, wanted to hear some of that, what they call his best moments supposedly, the part where he was playing so-called "Sheets of Sound,"
you know, he took it further than that.
Yes.

You know, he was searching to see how they played three notes at once. You can tell, if your ear is trained, you hear him make a run and he keeps repeating it. He's practicing. Not only on the stand, but off the stand as well. When he get through playing that set, you're in the dressing room, he's back there still running over his horn.
Right.
You know, used to make Elvin -- not Elvin so much; Elvin's a dynamo, he's a machine up there -- but Jimmy Garrison --
He would lay out.
They'd have to lay out. You know, what can you do?
McCoy (inaudible).

McCoy would have to lay out. He'd say, 'Where's he going?' Now, he didn't play for ninety hours (inaudible). Only two of them playing, that's Elvin and Trane, you know, but he had something to say. Well, a whole lot of the kids, well, that's it. So they jump up there and they start making those same kinds of noises, what they thought was noises, sound. You're not thinking of the technical ability of doing that. They figure that's it.
So, I would say that most of them are starting at the
top. They didn't want to crawl. They want to start at the top. Just play, just play. This is free.
Right.
It's free, all right.
But then Trane said that you were doing things that would be considered free within the structure, within the confines of the music you were playing in the Monk band.

Yeah, well, that was the point. Monk would get up and we could -- that's what I meant when I said go outside and inside. We knew where we were at. We knew the tunes, structure -- you know, could get back in. But we'd take it out as far as we wanted to take it out.
Right.
You know, I used to do that and just see how far I could go.
Right.

You know? Monk come back in, boom. We know where he's at. We had one chord and we was right back into the thing. That's so far as avantgarde -- I used to kind of run from them. The cats would say, 'Man, you play avantgarde.' It's like Dave [Higgins] would say, 'Man, you know, you're the first cat to play the avantgarde.' I wondered about that. I said, 'What are you talking about?' I didn't look at it like that. I didn't even know the meaning of the word, 'avantgarde.'
But that seems to have gone under now.
No, no, it's --
(Inaudible).
It's coming back. Look, they --

But don't you think people were preoccupied with the crossover, what they call crossover, like Edwin Newman said: 'If I could get rid of words, Edward (unintelligible). That's one of the crossover. them --'
(Laughter.)

People were preoccupied with what they were calling crossover, jazz rock and they weren't talking so much about avantgarde. But at those concerts, Cecil Taylor will still sell out and there they will be young college kids.
If you notice, though, it's Cecil Taylor all alone.
Solo.
You know? And Keith Jarrett is coming down to that actually. It's a form of, to me, European, classical, you know? But they have never learned to call it jazz.
(Laughter.)

You know, what's that about? You know? But that's where it's going. It's all about money. In order to play on the big concert stage, if you're not playing the rock thing, you've got to play the thing like Chick Corea or Keith Jarrett or any of those groups -- Cecil Taylor -- you know.
Look at this thing they did not too long ago -- Marylou and --
And Cecil.
-- and Cecil at Carnegie Hall, you know?
Well, I guess she was curious.
She was curious just to see what would happen.
But then he --
He did it all alone. She had a bass and drummer with her. But Cecil just did his thing. That's him. He knows. But he's making good money at that.
Oh, yeah.
It's all about economics, period. Who can make the most money, you know.
When you were coming up, it seems that people did it for the love of playing.

Well, that was the whole thing. That's another thing I admire about Thelonius. He was saying something -- Patrick asked him, say, "Man, what do you think about the music? Monk said, 'It's so fast, it took the beauty out of music?' Actually, he doesn't want to play anymore.
Does not (inaudible).
You know? I was thankful that we were able to go up there and catch him at the Carnegie and that whole house was 90 percent packed with white college-age kids.
Right.
The hall was sold out. And he Thelonius was so beautiful, so beautiful. He hasn't played.
It just makes you wish, though, that you always want to see people with that kind of ability and the ideal circumstances --
Circumstances.
-- and you never see them under ideal circumstances.

No, either they're in some little smoke-infested hall, you know, standing in the bathroom with no dressing room, nothing to cool out, or either standing outside, catching pneumonia. Oh, well, that's a sign of the times.
If you had your choice of things that you like to play, what kinds of things would you say you really enjoy playing?

Well, I just enjoy straight-ahead music. What I mean by "straight-ahead" is pick a tune with some changes and within those changes, do whatever we wanted to. I like form. That's my personal thing. I loved listening to Ray Brown do it and, oh, so many people -- Sam Jones -- talking about bass players -- Cecil McBee (PHONETIC) goes out a little bit.
What about people like Bob Cranshaw, Victor Gaskin?
Cranshaw is heavy, heavy. Cranshaw is
heavy.
He said something about you once that I thought was significant.
Oh.
He was working at the Cellar in New York with Al Foster and --
And Monty, yeah.

-- Monty Alexander, and he said that he had a fiddle once that he just couldn't play. It was just a hard instrument to play. He had just about decided to get rid of it and he let you use it, he let you play it, and he heard you play it and it made him keep that instrument.
(Laughter.)
He was talking about how you could play any instrument, just walk up and pick up a fiddle and play it.
That's me.
How do you account for that?

Well, I don't know. Like I said, I very seldom -- I didn't own a fiddle often, you know, so I had to play whatever I could get my hands on. In doing so, I had to learn how to make it sound like a fiddle should sound, you know, so that was all. It was just in your touch. Now, just like we got all kinds of little gimmicks, you know, wah-wah pedals and all that kind of stuff. We used to do it with your fingers, you know, your wrist. Oh, that's what I mean by working at it
and you enjoy playing when you're working at something. Naturally, working at, say, you're a teacher and you have to type out lessons and whatnot. You enjoy doing that, don't you?
Well, I enjoy the result of it.
That's what I'm talking about, uh-huh.
I enjoy that, yeah.

Well, it's the same thing with my instrument, to be able to make it sing, and to be able to watch somebody's expression while you're playing, to see whether he's actually -- whether you can make him or her, whatever, aware of what you're doing. I've been able to do it through the years. So I'm just happy that I had a gift from the Master, God. He give me a gift and I put it to use.

It's also said that a tune like "All the Things You Are" on that More from the Vanguard is your ideal tempo. It's clear that you have an accurate sense of tempo of tunes that -- for instance, you seem to feel the tempo as an organic part of the tune itself, so you wouldn't play "Cherokee" real slow and around Midnight, real fast, although I've heard it done. How do you arrive -- how did you arrive at this sense of an ideal tempo? Was that just playing all these different tunes that you talked about? (Inaudible)?
It could be playing for dances, you know? I'll tell you a band -- a couple of bands, big bands -- the idea of big bands is to play dance music. They had solos. They might

take a little solo or eight bars and half a chorus, but there was some people dancing. Lunceford's band was beautiful. Basie's band was beautiful, too, and all the bands -- Benny Goodman, Artie Shaw, Glenn Miller -- all those people had dance bands. But you had to know tempos, also.

I worked with a fellow -- I'm not going to call his name because I respect him so much -- but he had what's known as a "happy foot" or a "frantic foot." Now, he would take "Stardust" and if you don't watch him, he'd be playing it as fast as you would "Tiger Rag" or something. He'd stomp it off, you know, nervous foot.
Just keep accelerating.
Well, no, he'd stomp it off too fast.
Oh, uh-huh.
And once he's out there, you got to play it.
Play it then, yeah.
You know, and some people don't have no idea of tempos for certain tunes, you know.
Right, that's true.

Sometimes, they say, "We're going to play a ballad," they'd stomp it off so slow, it's not even worth playing. You know, you'd be tired before you'd play the first chorus. It's all in having a knack for sense of timing. I like it because I was able to dance, just to get the feel of it.
Do you see yourself -- you talked about how Paul has influenced the, you know, the bassists. (inaudible). How do you see yourself as having influenced?

Well, I can't say. I've heard people say they've been influenced by me, a whole lot of them. It's gratifying and I've listened for certain things that I used to do, I can hear in some cats. You know, but like the way bass players are going now, I don't hear it as much, but I hear it in an extension of Paul Chambers, you know, which is beautiful.
(Recording interruption.)

-- think feeling -- you talk about feelings being very important. For instance, in the thing that Valerie Wilmer (phonetic) did, In The Face of The Black Music, it comes off that you think feeling in music is very important. With the electronics taking over, how do you think feeling can be preserved or will it be preserved at all?

I don't see how it can be preserved with electronics. Electronics is cold. There's no feeling there. It's coming over a wire. You can't control it unless you got the button, whether you turn it up and down, loud and soft. But I mean, just that body feeling is hard.
Do you think -- well, particularly black musicians -- do you think it'll ever go back to the church? Because as long as that exists, it seems like the feeling will exist.

Well, almost everything you hear now in the so-called rock is churchy. You can go from any church, any Baptist church, any church, you hear the same set-up, same set-up musically. The back-up singers, just like the choir.

Well, I noticed that -- well, now, it's coming up -- people would use electric guitar (inaudible) other instruments. But the only electrified instruments were occasionally electric piano, but organ and electric guitar. But now, they have full rock and roll band amps.
Oh, yeah.
And everything.

The public can't see unless you got an amplifier. They don't believe that you can play without having one. The public's ears are messed up and if you're playing acoustic, they'll tell you they can't hear you. You're playing too soft, because they've been bombarded with all this sound.

But I don't know. It seems that it should be able to be -- it should be complementary. For instance, now in the '50s, gospel music. You may have somebody like Drink Small (ABONETIO), who used to play spiritual hymns and he'd have amplifiers. But the physical presence of the people themselves and their voices, it wasn't about the amplification. It was about the singers moreso. So that was supposed to complement. Do you think they will ever reach that
I really don't know. I really don't know. Actually, I don't know.
What about the different personalities of cities? People talk about Kansas City and Chicago, New York.

Well, to tell you the truth, I can't say much about Kansas City or any other cities, you know, St. Louis. I was through there while I was in service. I never did play St. Louis, Kansas City, New Orleans. Never played California. But that's all on me. So, I couldn't say. Now, I played from people from those cities. That's a different thing, you know.

In my hometown at one time, like I said, I'm not saying it because it was just my hometown, but it was a swinging place, because there was so much happening there, at the time, being the rail here, there weren't too many people wasn't flying during those days. They was riding trains, you know, or cars or buses. They'd link up in Chicago. That was something.
Enormous stockyard.
Yeah, uh-huh. Well, that's why I say, it was a rail here, head, you know? Center of the country.
What were some of the other places that you played with Monk in the '70s?
Well, we went to Toronto -- supposed to have been a two-week gig. That gig, Eddie Blackwell wasn't with us then. He had Beaver Harris (PHONETIC) and he asked me

to get a tenor player, so I got Pat Patrick. Pat had been working with Sun Ra. I knew him from Chicago -- and myself. So we went to Toronto and while there, (unintelligible) in the band come in, play with the Toronto Symphony. We all were staying at the King Edward Hotel there in Toronto. We were working at the Colonial Room and Duke loved to play, and Monk (unintelligible) from the hotel, he and his wife Nellie, Monk locked the door and you can't get to see him until it's time to go to work.

I understand Duke was knocking on Monk's door. "Hey, it's Duke." Monk wouldn't answer him. He said -- Duke wanted to play, you know. Duke was just jamming all the time, you know. That's his thing. However, I was talking to Willie Cook and Paul Gonzalves, people like that -- John Hodges -- I had met him, and I think Cat Anderson was in the band.
(Recording interruption.)

Cat Anderson was in the band, and Julian Priestley and I went down just before we went to work, we went down to Masie Hall where they were getting it together, you know, Joe Benjamin. Duke Ellington's valet, a friend of mine, he said, "Man, I want you to meet Duke." I said, "Well, I met Duke before," which I had out in Chicago, back in the '60s. Paul and I were hanging out one night at E. Parker McDougall (PHONETIC) and Paul Gonzalves say, "Man, you probably bring

Wilbur down to the studio," -- we recording down there tomorrow -- he says, "I want Duke to hear him." (Unintelligible) John Lamb was playing bass with him and they were talking about trying to get me in the band. Well, I was crazy to (unintelligible) accept a gig because I had too much respect for Duke, you know, to get in the band and know he'd be writing music and all that and I couldn't read it. However, the cat was telling me, say, "Man, Duke don't write no music for basses, you know, unless he's got a special concert or something like that."

But anyway, I go, and he's sitting around and they were recording and Duke, in between while they was changing tapes, Duke's playing the piano, you know, and the rest of the cats are milling around and John Lamb was standing up there with his (unintelligible) bass -- Duke's playing something like the blues. I asked John, "Let me play along with Duke," and I did. I enjoyed that very much. Duke looked up from the piano, just kept playing, looked at me, and we had a good little rapport. I didn't have a chance to say nothing to him because we had to go right into the numbers. When I come out of the studio, we walked to the little rest area, Johnny approached me, John Hodges (unintelligible) looking kind of strange. He shook my hand, you know. I was really in awe of the guy. He was so great. Real giants, I had always looked up to that band and Carney, Cootie, everybody. It was just marvelous being in their presence.
So, up in Toronto, I go, like I say, we go over there, (unintelligible)

try to catch part of a performance before we started work that night. It was our last night in Toronto and do you know that Duke came around while we were playing -- most of the guys in the band -- there was Cat Anderson, Johnny Hodges and his wife, and the greatest thing, the feeling, that Johnny -- I mean, it was just love, that I was standing talking to Monk getting ready to come up on the bandstand and at the Colonial, they had a mezzanine up there, where you had coffee and you could look down on the stage.

Johnny walked all the way around to me and Thelonius and he said, "Wilbur, would you come over here? I want you to meet my wife." To me, that was one of the world's greatest compliments, took the time for him to say he wanted me to meet his wife. I walked around there. He introduced me to her and that's the last time I saw him, because it wasn't long after that time that Johnny he passed away.
That he died. That was in 1970.

1970, that's true. However, I found out later that the Duke Ellington Orchestra when they needed a bass player, they would call my house for me. You know, I was usually out somewhere. I missed a couple of gigs. But the cats told me, they say, "Man, you should have come on with the band," and that would have been my biggest, greatest thrill, you might say, because I had always wanted to play with that band.
But getting back to the Monk, we left Toronto and

come back to New York. I think we played a week down at the Vanguard and then we had another gig up in Boston. Same group -- Pat Patrick, Beaver Harris, myself. We get to Boston and it's during the time that Globe Newspaper had a festival. They had all the big names -- Sarah, Erroll Garner, Miles Davis. Miles had Chick Corea, Jack DeJohnette --
: (Inaudible).

No, Jack DeJohnette. I think Wayne Shorter was with the band. It was either Wayne or George Coleman. However, we're playing at this club -- what do they call that club? Well-known jazz club in Boston. Anyway, all these musicians come over after their shows, you know, and Beaver was (inaudible) down that night.
(Laughter.)

He had went up to the Zildjian cymbal house and got a whole lot of cymbals and a great big gong. So he had it in his head when the announcer announced Thelonius, "Thelonius Monk," you know, come on the stand, we would step out on the bandstand. Beaver sit down and I take my (inaudible) the bass and Beaver would draw back with this mallet. He's going to hit the gong and he missed the whole gong. Very embarrassing, but you know, people in the club was very stiff. They was, you know, but Monk was very angry by having that.
So, when we got back -- well, I mean. I want to tell you something else. I hadn't seen Erroll Garner in years

up close, but he come in and he saw me come right down in front, he was a powerful little cat, just picked me up bodily and just -- oh, (unintelligible), you George Duvivier know, glad to see me and I was happy to see him -- (inaudible), cats like that.

Anyway, we get back to New York and Thelonius let Beaver people go. So he asked me to get a drummer and I got Leroy Williams, another home drummer. He's currently been working with Barry Harris, Charles McPherson, and the next job we have, Pat Patrick had to leave, so we got Paul Jeffries. We played Raleigh, North Carolina. We come back from Raleigh and played the Vanguard and that was the last gig I played with Thelonius. No, we played one gig down in Chinatown, New York, little concert for one of them Chinese boys clubs like.
But that was about the last gig I had with Thelonius.

During this period, Red Garland comes through New York. Philly Jimmy Joe Jones, myself and Red Garland played a little East Side joint, little jazz joint, up in the 90s. That place was really diggin' it, but cat wouldn't take care of business. The cat would come in at 12:00 and play until three and that was it, you know. So, that didn't last long and Archie Shepp had some more (unintelligible) gigs for me. He say, "Well, come on, Wilbur, let's go down to Philly" -- about 72 -- and coming down here to play at a place called Aqua Lounge over in West Philly. Archie had Maged, Charles Greenlee on trombone. He had Dave Burrell on piano and Joe Masontos (PHONETIC) on congar and
Ali
Ottie on congas and Beaver Harris on drums. That was his band.

I hadn't been down there since the '60s. But I played. We played that weekend and that's where I met my wife Gloria. She was sitting there at the bar, loved music and we talked for -- a musician that knew me introduced me to her. I didn't know she was a schoolteacher or nothing like that. She was just a lady and kind enough to put -- she knew Dave Burrell. She knew Dave and his wife. So, she said, "Well, instead of commuting back to New York, why don't you stay out at my house?" I said, "Me, too?" She said, "Of course." So, we come and spent the weekend with her. I told her, "If you ever come to New York, look me up," you know. I'd like to repay her for her hospitality.
That's what happened. That was our meeting, we've been together just about ever since then. That's for you, honey.
(Laughter.)
Yes.
But anyway, let me see. Archie had another gig. He had Carnegie Hall and he used me, he used --
(Inaudible) That was Newport.
No, Carnegie Hall.
Newport. Wasn't that part of the Newport Festival of '72?
It might have been.
Yes.
I forgot, yeah, because they had all acts, different acts. That's true. He had Billy Green in a solo spot. He had Cal Massey on a solo spot. He had Beaver and he had Dave Burrell.
C Sharpe

C Sharpe and his wife China. This was all part of Archie Shepp's grouping. It was nice. A nice little show. Then I run into an old friend I hadn't seen, pianist-composer Bobby Scott. He'd come in, you know, I hadn't seen him since 1957, I think, or '58, something like that. So, it was a beautiful time. So that was in '72 and that's when I did -- the same time I did that record date for Paul Jeffrey, Stanley Clarke, all these other cats, you know, about ten musicians.

Then I moved up to Brooklyn, moved out to the house that Billy Higgins, drummer, was living in. Gloria and I took a ground-floor apartment and moved the furniture from Philly over there -- piano and everything. But by then, I was drinking this vodka like it was going out of style and Gloria started seeing what it was doing to me and suggested, 'Let's get into A.A.' She join Al-Anon. Tried that and tried it. I failed. Kept trying. During this period, Blackwell called me up. He had a job for me up at Amherst. It was beautiful. You know, they had something like a weekend semin-

ar, workshop. He had Nathan Davis, Dr. Nathan Davis, from the University of Pittsburgh on tenor. We had Clifford Clifton Thornton -- well, Clifford played some kind of East Indian instrument. Bill Cole was the major voice in giving this.
Organizer.

Organizing it. There was Vishnu Wood, Bill Wood on bass -- two basses, Eddie Blackwell and the three horns. I played -- just had one little concert, got my money, come on back to Brooklyn. The next job I had was down here at community college, Billy Higgins and I brought a group down. Played for the students through the help of Gloria and the Black Students League. Dee Dee Bridgewater was supposed to make it with us, but she had a prior engagement. So we brought Roland Alexander, Riane Kenny Zawadi and --
Claude Bartee.

On tenor. Two tenors and we had a swinging time. Then -- what happened during that period? Oh, that's the time that my health really started failing. I wouldn't stop smoking cigarettes and I went to see the doctor. In fact, my lungs had been weak. He told me, 'I think you have emphysema.' That really didn't frighten me because I was fighting this alcohol and A.A. I'd make it a day or two and slip. I started having convulsions. Well, I was in kind of bad shape.
However, with the help of my wife, I got over. I

came through pretty good. And I worked -- for a while, while I was working -- I'm going to get back to something. I was working with Thelonius, we had another job. I got a job -- this was before I met Gloria -- working as a counselor in one of those methadone drug abuse programs and that's when I went back with Thelonius again. Only this time, we had Philly Joe Jeffrey Jones on drums, Paul Jeffries on tenor and myself. We was working opposite Blood, Sweat and Tears.

We had a job in Philharmonic Hall and that was kind of weird. All these electronic Blood, Sweat and Tears and the Thelonius Monk acoustic quartet. But we played and I had this job, like I said, as a counselor. I worked at it about three months. Monk said, "Well, we got to go up to Quebec." We had a job up there, university, Canada. On our way back, we were to play the Arena in Washington. Syracuse. We played the University of Syracuse with that same group -- Philly Billy Joe, Paul and myself.
Let's see. That was about the end of the Thelonius Monk gigs.
But you had come down here from Brooklyn to Philadelphia to live.
Yeah, uh-huh. I had to get away from -- had to follow you on down. You (inaudible). So I was following my wife, you know.
And how about living and working in
Philadelphia?

Well, to me, it's ideal, to get from Philly to New York. You know, this is kind of away from all that ratrace in New York and if you can gig, you can go up to New York and record, come on back home. Well, you know what's been happening now, I've been working with Clifford Jordan on and off, say, back in '76, before I really got ill. We played, Cliff and I, we worked Guadalupe, (unintelligible) club they had. No, first we went to Detroit for ten days. We had Roy Burrowes on trumpet, George (unintelligible) on drums, Clifford Jordan and myself. Pianoleess quartet. We worked ten days out there at the keystone -- no, the Keyboard Lounge.
Baker's Keyboard Loung.

And then we played a college out there, a concert. Come on back to Philly and he went on back up to New York and Clifford called me up, said, "We got a record date." We did a record date for Muse. Was just released this year. It's called "Remembering Me," with the same personnel except we had Chris Anderson, blind Chris Anderson, playing piano. We had some vocals on there. A young man named Hank Diamond Smith that put words to "Prayer to the People," one of Clifford's arrangements, and the Powerful Paul Robeson, another Clifford tune.
Incidentally, we had Clifford's daughter Donna singing and Thelonius Monk's daughter Boo-boo. Maybe you'll
get a chance to hear that one of these days. It's been out, like I said, a few months now.
But anyway, after that record date and Detroit gig, Cliff called me one day and said, 'Well, man, we got five days in Chicago.' Now, that was last --
It's been over a year.
Over a year. That was in '76. Around October, wasn't it?
September.

MR. WARE: September. Anyway, I went out there but I was feeling very ill. I could hardly carry my instrument and I was gasping for breath. We were to play with Kenny Clarke. Kenny Clarke. It was going to be one of his first gigs. He had come over to me that reunion, TV show that Public Broadcasting Station out there, which he did with Dizzy and Moody, Sarah, Milt, Al Haug, Ray Brown. So Al Haug and Klook stayed out there and Clifford and myself, we went out for Joe Sagal to form a quartet. We played at the Jazz Showcase (inaudible).

I made it, though. I wasn't comfortable at all. I could hardly -- I played, but I was gasping for breath. I was like a fish out of water. I wasn't under the correct medication. So I got on the plane coming home. I just didn't make it home. I was home up until I had a job here in Philly called At the Foxhole and I was going to use Clifford --
Wilbur Campbell.
Wilbur Campbell, drummer, from home. He come up and make the gig with us, two nights.
Sam Dockery

Sam Dockery on piano and we had a surprise guest, Babs Gonzales come up, just to sing with us. But before this could come about, my lung collapsed on me. It frightened me, but stayed in the hospital for about seven or eight days and they inflated it again and I felt good, better than I did in months, because they put me on the proper medication. Do you know, I was tipping around there, sneaking cigarettes? The man had told me to stop smoking as early as 1973. But I didn't, so I paid the price.
Now after we played the gig, the gig was in November -- was it November?
In Chicago?
No, --
At the Foxhole. That was November, yes.

November. After we played the gig, Christmas was coming up. Christmas Eve, my lung collapsed again and that really frightened me. So, I've been very cool. The man says I've got to take it very easy, you know. It's a slow process. I can make it, but I've got to take it easy.
However, did all right up until about a month ago. Collapsed again. So I'm just getting over it. Taking it easy.
Well, that's really all you've worked in
this area, the Foxhole with Clifford.
Oh, I made that record date with Walt Dixon Dickerson.
Two of those.

Two of those, with the Japanese company (unintelligible). The records -- Why Not. That's about it. (Unintelligible) jobs around. I've been down to the college and talked to the kids about black music.
I noticed you were talking about, towards the end, the college dates that people are working, that you were working with Monk. There seemed to be a trend more in the '70s.

It is. The college kids are very aware of what had been before them. They didn't get a chance to hear it like we did as high school kids because it's not in the theaters like it used to be. So most of the concerts they do see, they have to go to New York to catch the Newport things or some big concert. They only see one side of it, whoever the promoter is pushing, you know. They don't see people that they've been hearing about for years.

So, they're running courses on it. The colleges are hiring people, you know, artists in residence, to bring the music to them. They are eating it up. They are really getting into it. You know, like Dave Baker was telling us?
Yes, yes, indeed. There have been other people working around here in Philadelphia, but a lot of good
musicians came out of Philadelphia.
A whole lot of them. Some of the best.
And there are lots of musicians here that don't really have work, don't have things to do.

There's no place to work, really, and the -- it boils down to this. In your hometown, you're a local musician -- I don't care how much music you can play -- you're just old Joe -- "Oh, that's old Joe." They'll walk past you to get to somebody that's coming out of New York. Whoever's coming out of New York, he might not play as good as old Joe, but the man say, "Oh, he's from New York." That's been going on for years. That's the same thing, out at my hometown, when I was -- during the '50s and '40s, say, "Oh, that's old Wilbur," you know. Yeah, but after I went to New York, my goodness.
Oh, uh-huh.
They was, "Ooh, Wilbur? Where? That's my buddy."
When we went there in -- I guess that was '75, and they were having a memorial for Gene Hammonds (PHONETIC) at --
Cadillac Bob's (PHONETIC).
-- Cadillac Bob's. And Lucky Carmichael and Dr. Joe-Joe Adams and --
Vernell.
Fournier, John Young, (unintelligible),

-- Vernelly, (unintelligible), and the other singer whose name escapes me at the moment -- it'll come to me. But it was just -- everybody seemed so happy to see you and they asked me to stand up, take a bow, here's Wilbur home. It was a different feeling then. They seemed proud.

That's the way it is. You know, you go away from your hometown and just make a record or two or get a little recognition that somebody read about you and you're a celebrity. I used to think, 'Well, I'm playing the same stuff I was playing (inaudible). Why do you treat me this way now?' You know?

Well, in the '50s, I notice even myself, in the '50s, when we were coming up, rock and roll was getting to be a thing that was being pushed, but you could still walk in the clubs and hear Billie Holiday or Charlie Parker on the jukebox. It was still available to you, even though rock and roll was being pushed more and more.

Well, let me tell you about that now. There are clubs -- just like Slugs -- they playing all that -- you know, when it was open -- playing all that good music in there -- Lee Morgan Marvin, that's where he died at -- playing and when he'd get off the stand, they'd turn on the jukebox and they got all this rock music on. That was a musician that would get off the bandstand and have earplugs in their ears or they'd have to go outside, because they can't stand to hear

the music. That's a heck of a contrast, you know. But that's the way it does. You hear that on the radio all day long. All you hear is the rock thing. All the stations -- AM, most FM stations -- might have one station that has --
Disco they is call it now.

One station that's playing pure jazz and it's usually a college station, you know. Even New York, they only have one station and for a while, they was pure jazz. That was WRVR. But now, what they're playing is what they call the fusion, crossover. But that's a sign of the times.
Well, where do you think the music is heading? Where do you think it's going?

That's hard to say. I hear some awful beautiful things coming out of the electric groups -- electronics. It's got to go up. It won't go back. They'll incorporate it some kind of way. Either you will play all acoustic or you will play all electronics. That's all I can say about it.
Well, with all the categories, where does it leave people like Cliff that is still trying to play?

Well, Clifford, now. You take a cat like Clifford. He did something recently. I don't think it's released yet. He and Dizzy Reese, Richard Davis, Mahal, Richard Abrams -- he's got a tuba in there. Might be Bob

Stewart or Howard Johnson and the old boy sounds so beautiful. Beautiful. I heard the taping of it. I'm just waiting on it. But like you said, where is the music going? Who knows? Somebody's got to step out and lead. There's always been a leader, somebody step out in front. Thad has a leading band to me, you know.
Thad Bad Jones.

Thad Bad Jones, Mel Lewis. They were leading. Then there's Toshiko and Lew Tabackin-- their band is pretty heavy. That's the big band. There's Grover Washington, Jr. I heard some of the things he did recently.
Well, they've ganna change. As the times change, you think they will change.

They've got to. But it has to do with energy, too, you know, like you made a statement earlier about pulling the plug. They can't be hooking up those amplifiers too consistently. Who knows? Who knows what the future holds as far as music's concerned.

Well, more and more people are thinking about music education in terms of black music. It's like this tape. People are thinking about it in schools. But people that have had to learn the way you learned are going to have to come up with new approaches because the ones now are not adequate.
Well, that's true. Then there are some cats still out there-- teaching Milt Hinton Henry, he's out there teaching.
Max Mack has been teaching. There's Larry Ridley (PHONETIC), bass player, kid over in Jersey, has been teaching.
(Inaudible)? No.
Thad's But they're teaching schools, you know, colleges.
(End of Side 3.)
Oh, boy.

It's not just music education, but all areas of education, that are going to have to change, because more people are becoming educated. It's the thing that you see years ago, for example, when it was hard to buy instruments and people played one instrument and they played it well and then if you saw a person playing two, it was really something. Nowadays, kids have all kinds of instruments -- three and four instruments they're playing. It's a different approach, a different student, and people are going to have to come over to different methods of teaching them different approaches of reaching them.

How can you see people being used, for instance, that haven't normally been thought of as teachers like yourself of other musicians that have normally just been musicians, players. But now they're going to have to somehow give that information to other people because the way that you got it is not available to the kids.
That's true. Not available. Well, it
boils down to individual being motivated, if he really wanted to learn, you know. Like you were speaking a moment ago about having more than one instrument. That reminded me of a certain master --
Jack of all trades and master of none.

Jack of all trades, master of none. That's true. It's the only one you can play well -- you can play the other, two or three or whatever, you know, but it's one you excel at, you know, they take a fella like Benny Carter. Collins. He could play trumpet as well as alto. Either one, you know. But he's remembered moreso for his alto.
Alto, yeah.
Yeah.
Same with Ira Sullivan, trumpet (inaudible).
Yeah.

But most good musicians have a knowledge of -- I think it's a (unintelligible) little different to have a knowledge of an instrument. For instance, you might see Philly Joe sitting at the piano or the saxophone, but his instrument is drums.

Drums, well, piano is percussive, too. Now, you catch a good arranger, he should be able to have a working knowledge of each instrument, you know. I don't know whether he should play them, but he should have a working
knowledge of them. A good arranger, you know, and there are some guys can write music just like you'd sit down and write a letter and cannot play an instrument, you know?

That's an area that's interesting about the difference between being able to play an instrument and to have a knowledge, technical knowledge of music. How do you see that difference? You talked about in terms of your not wanting to learn how to read, but now kids don't make that choice. They automatically learn how to read.

Uh-huh. I don't know what to tell you about. To me, it's -- I'm afraid to even dwell on it because I don't know nothing about it. Now, the person I wish were in my place right now to answer a question like that would be a bassist that I have the greatest respect for. That's Bill Lee. Bill can write. Everybody in his family is a good musician -- his sister. He's got a brother, younger brother -- I think he's a younger brother. But Bill -- I don't know whether you hear of that New York Bass Choir. Oh, he wrote --
Oh, I heard it.
-- some beautiful things, some beautiful things for that.
Yeah, I heard it.
And he's a beautiful musician, you know? But then you catch a cat that can write all kind of music, you know, all kind of -- I'll use the old term -- snakes and turns and

twists, brilliant. But he's got to have somebody to interpret his ideas. He's got to have somebody that can play his music, you know. There's Ernie Wilkins, good arranger. Quincy Jones is another. But he has to have the type of caliber musician to play it. It's like I say, Duke. Duke would write something for Johnny, because Johnny knew how to play it, you know. He couldn't write out the solo that Johnny would play, but Johnny would interpret his idea.
Interpret that in the way that he wanted.

He wanted. It would be just perfect because Duke could see Johnny playing an idea of his. Paul Gonzalves is another beautiful saxophonist. Ben Webster, Coleman Hawkins, Don Byas. I'm talking about saxophonists. You don't find them like that no more and it's funny because those guys -- I remember Ben made a statement that his whole idea when he was coming up was to play with a beautiful tone, you know, and it seems like kids have thrown that away. They don't strive for no sound, no pure sound. Most of them, they're so busy being so technical and everybody wanted to play fast, true, but you lose something in playing fast. You don't have no tone qualities. Some of them out there know how to use it, but not like in my day coming up.
Now, I'm saying that, look like I'm a diehard, because music moves on. It's true. But I love beautiful sounds. I love beautiful sounds. I was listening recently to a whole old

Duke Ellington 1940s band, the reeds section of Hodges, Otto Hardwick, Ben Webster, Harry Carney, Barney Bigard, -- to me, that was one of the greatest reed sections in the world. Then there was Jimmy Lunceford's That was (unintelligible) reed section. Another terrible reed section -- But, Thad and eh, but bad and Mel's reed section, very beautiful. It has been. But I don't know, like you say, where music is heading. It's hard to say. I'm going to go back a little bit.

I came down here -- I think it was '61 -- with Al Gray and Billy Mitchell. They had a sextet. We had a week at Peps, old Peps down there on Broad Street. He had a trumpet player -- I forgot the brother's name -- he also had arranger, Gene, who played piano as well as peck horn. That's an alto horn, looks something like your that euphonium that Kiane plays (unintelligible). But it blended, so that meant we had four horns and his drums and bass on certain arrangements. It was beautiful, beautiful sound. I stayed with the band and we played that week and went back to New York and come back down here.

It was the following weekend, they played some clubs and we come down to play for -- they had some -- some young disc jockey around here had a -- trying out for a TV show. He had the Jimmy Smith organ trio, Don Schwartz and Donald Bailey on drums -- the original Jimmy Smith.
With Eddie Fadden
He wasn't with them. It was Thornel. Farnell.

We played a TV show and what made me feel so good, Nat Cole was in town and he didn't play, but he was a guest, you know, and this guy was questioning him. We played out two or three tunes and I had played opposite Nat Cole back in '53, down at the old Blue Note. It was called Lips Low Level then in Chicago. Nat had Charles Norris on bass, John Collins, guitar and Lee Young on drums and himself on piano. We played our set and Nat (unintelligible) would bring his group. I noticed he used to come out and watch us. The cat I was working with was Buster Bennett and Robert Montgomery, just the three of us -- saxophone, bass and piano.

Buster was playing sock cymbal to give us a little leverage, you know, and it seemed like Nat marveled at that. I spoke to him just once -- and like I say, I didn't know of him -- but he remembered me in Philly here in '61 because when we finished the show, they had featured me on the last tune, and I had a little thing I did on Lester Young's "Lester Leaps In," and my solo work, you know. So when I finished, and we were standing there, Nat got up from the dais where he was sitting and started toward the band. So naturally, Al and Billy Mitchell (unintelligible), but he just walked past Al and and Billy grabbed my hand and said, "Man, I certainly enjoyed that." He say, "I know you." And I told him, you know, where it was. He said, "What happened to you?" Al had asked him for an autographed picture of himself and I went

to sleep and we had a matinee that Sunday and I didn't make the gig and he said, "I looked for you and you didn't show up that night. What happened?" So that was just one time, but Al Gray teases me now. He says, "Yeah, here's the only cat, Nat Cole walked over and shook his hand instead of my hand and I'm the leader of the band."
But I enjoyed those little things. But I had a chance to -- you know Ezzard Charles, the late Ezzard Charles?
Edward Charles, yeah.
Yeah, he was come into the Bohemia. (unintelligible).
From Camden, I think, wasn't he?
No, I think he was from Cincinnati.
Ezzard Edward Charles, uh-huh.
You're thinking about the commissioner here.
Yeah.
What's the old man's name? He was a champ, too.
I know, right.
Joe. Jersey Joe.
Jersey Joe Walcott, right.

But Ezzard Edward was from Cincinnati and he used to play bass around Cincinnati. My dad told me that. I'm playing down at the Bohemia, come up, stayed one night. He's standing in the middle of the bar and the owner say, "It's
Ezzard Charles want
(unintelligible) talk to you." I walked up to him. He says, "Man, I like your bass playing. Do you think you could teach me some?"
(Laughter.)

I said, yeah, but I didn't want to (inaudible). I feel like I would be a bad influence and maybe some of his people would, you know, his promoter might run me off because I wasn't clean at all. I had that, you know, thought in my mind. So. But it's nice to know that people are watching you that you never would feel --
That's true.
-- that's looking at you.

Archie Moore, he was in, you know, and he shook my hand and cats that you wouldn't think are interested in what you're doing. Not trying to showboat so much, just real people, you know? I always keep that remembrance as long as I can -- I always keep that fond remembrance.
(Laughter.)
When you think back, are there any highlights or any significant things that you haven't thought of that you didn't get a chance to mention? There's so much.

There's so much. It's hard to try to just pick something out, you know, to say. But I want to tell you something funny, though. In our hustling days, back there in the '30s, we went out with the tramp band one

night. We had this long -- we'd hired somebody with a touring car. I don't know, one of them old Buicks, had running board on it. We out there on, past Cicero, and one of them roadhouse taverns like -- one of the guys go in and ask the man, "Could we come in and play?" He says, "No, no, we don't want you in here." But the customers said, "Yeah, come on." So, we just struck up right there outside of the club and we're out there just playing our little Tiger Rag, (unintelligible), and the people clapping and putting money in our hat. The owner come out of the back door and he had a machine gun.
(Laughter.)
He started firing up in the air. We started running. Can you imagine me running with that big homemade fiddle? And the guy had the car, driving off.
(Laughter.)
People got more kicks out of that. But it was frightening. That's the kind of things we had to go through. You know, I can think of some hilarious scenes.
Now, they seem -- in retrospect, they seem funny. But having lived through those.
It's like (unintelligible) little tavern, doing our number. Here's a lady with a little dog and I think it was Phineas -- he's out in front doing the mugging and dancing --
Newborn? Newborn?
No, (unintelligible) Henderson.
(Unintelligible). Phineas Henderson
Bill Henderson's older brother mounted his legs; (Unintelligible). He was dancing. This dog (unintelligible) growling.
(Laughter.)
And we still singing.
Still singing.

Oh, the stories can go on about the things that happened to musicians. When you look back on it now and laugh, but been some mean things. Musicians, entertainers, they'd pay double. I don't care what happen, you know, you might work all night, club owner say, "Well, you ain't got no money coming Who are you gonna turn money A" (Unintelligible) tell that to?
It's a strange --
(Inaudible) beat work you to death.
Yeah. It seems incredible, but if can work all your life and can't prove you worked --
Oh, that is --
-- at all, you can't --
-- you know, you worked steady and the man's steadily taking social security out and all that, and no record of it.
No.
You know? We have our unions and you know,

unless you working at what they call Class A clubs all your life, which isn't possible, even when they start making [segregated] locals in all the cities, across this great nation of ours, you had the dregs of the clubs. You worked all week and the cat disappears pay night and ain't nobody else supposed to come in there and play. The guy can turn his club over to his sister-in-law. You can't prove that.
It seems to me just astounding that --
Guys could survive.

-- the guys could survive at it and people, geniuses, could survive that. I hear people talking about Bird and drugs or something. But the fact that he could play so much music under those conditions --
Conditions.

-- is phenemonal. It has happened. He was damned by not only the fellas he played with, but some of the people that he played for, because they were the people that was feeding off him. Oh, shoot, we had -- I had guys, you know, on the road -- they'd follow us from engagement to engagement. The man was going to be there with the stuff, you know, and I worked one club out there in Chicago, the guy would sit right there. I think I was making ten dollars a night. See, that's $60 for six nights, and $60 I owe him.
Right.
Couldn't pay my rent. And he wants his
money.
But yet and still, you're supposed to be, in one sense, the ambassador, you know.

We loved our music, but there are certain elements that hate musicians and entertainers. Certain elements think that you just come in there to take a girl. Some young ladies love to be with an entertainer. He's fun and some of them flashy dressers, you know, and it makes them feel good. And then there's the guys (Unintelligible) if you don't wait outside and hit you with a baseball bat and beat you up, might kill you. You're going to spread a campaign, you know, go to the man, get you fired. Oh, it's mean and yet you got to get up there every night.

It's like when Mrs. Turner died, I was out trying to find, before I went to work that night, trying to find to beg the clubowner for (unintelligible) an advance so I could get my little fix and everybody's beating a path to my door to tell me Mrs. Turner died. I finally got on home. I had to get back to work. And I had to work. So, I worked that night though because it was my heart was breaking, house (unintelligible) but that's the way it is, you know.
Like they say, how does that song -- "Laugh, Clown, Laugh?" Pagliacci?
Uh-huh.
Well, it's true. Person up there entertaining, John Q., he doesn't realize that man's got the same
problems that he come in the club to forget.

Moreso in some instances because how you can be expected to take that kind of abuse and still create and support yourself, support a family, that's just out of the question. People have to be teaching, like now. Like Babs talks about getting a job. He makes it seem like a joke, but it's important that he's teaching in college. Archie Shepp at Amherst, Max Roach at Amherst -- those kind of jobs just didn't happen years ago.

Oh, no, no. Since they're very hard to come by now, you know, they try to curtail it. I don't know whether they're being ashamed -- the way I understand it, the Europeans have had it for years. You an artist, you an artist. You get paid for your art. Of course, you're giving it to the world. You creating things. In America, that's the system. You don't have a dollar, you're in trouble. Like I was saying, 'Here come these old horntooters. They ain't got no money.' You got to come into town, say, 'Well, can we stay here? We're going to play at such and such a club and we'll pay you at the end of the week.' Some people just -- you know, they good enough to know that we would pay or they go to the clubowner and says, 'I want my money.' You stand for it. So, we'd have a place to stay.
But we loved to play music. That's what I knew. That was my trade. I wouldn't change it for nothing in the
world. It has been a beautiful life. Still is. Let's hope I can fit in someway, you know.
Is there anything that you'd like to say that would close out?

Well, I'd like to call this little thing "Down Through the Years." Clifford Jordan, like I was speaking about this album that we made and I really love that album, "Starting Time." We did a tune that Cliff wrote called -- it's a ballad called "Down Through the Years." I think it would be nice if we can close out with that. Would you put it on, baby?
(Music.)
